chapters.title: Unit 1: The Last Address of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH)

lessons.title: The Last Address of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
The Last Address (the Farewell Sermon) of Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) is described in the book as the first and most important declaration regarding human rights. It is a comprehensive manifesto of human rights and a complete code of life for mankind, presenting not only rights but also responsibilities — rights do not exist without mutual responsibility among humankind. The Prophet (peace be upon him) delivered this sermon to the Muslims on the occasion of the last Hajj, in the valley of Arafat, Makkah, in February 632 A.D. (10 Zil Hajjah, 10 A.H.).

Listen and Pass On the Message

After praising and thanking Allah, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "O people, listen to me attentively, for I know not whether, after this year, I shall ever be amongst you again. Therefore, listen to what I am saying to you very carefully and take these words to those who could not be present here today."

Life and Property Are Sacred

Just as the people regard that month and that day as sacred, so they must regard the life and property of every Muslim as a sacred trust. Goods entrusted to anyone must be returned to their rightful owners. "Harm no one so that no one may harm you." Everyone will meet his Lord, and He will reckon his deeds.

Interest (Usury) Is Forbidden

Allah has forbidden taking usury (interest); therefore all interest obligations shall henceforth be waived. The capital, however, remains one's own to keep: "You will neither inflict nor suffer inequity." Allah has judged that there shall be no interest, and all the interest due to Abbas ibn Abd'al Muttalib shall henceforth be waived.

Beware of Satan

"Beware of Satan, for the safety of your religion. He has lost all hope that he will ever be able to lead you astray in big things, so beware of following him in small things."

The Rights of Women

Men have certain rights with regard to their women, and women also have rights over them. The men have taken them as wives only under Allah's trust and with His permission. "Do treat your women well and be kind to them, for they are your partners and committed helpers." Wives who abide by their husbands' rights deserve to be fed and clothed in kindness; and it is the husband's right that they do not make friends with anyone of whom he does not approve, and that they never be unchaste.

Worship and the Pillars of Islam

"O people, listen to me in earnest: worship Allah, perform your five daily prayers (Salah), fast during the month of Ramadan, and give of your wealth the poor due (Zakat). Perform Hajj (pilgrimage) if you can afford to."

Equality of All Mankind

"All mankind is from Adam, and an Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab; also a white has no superiority over a black, nor a black over a white, except by piety and good action." Every Muslim is a brother to every Muslim, and the Muslims constitute one brotherhood. Nothing that belongs to a fellow Muslim is legitimate for a Muslim unless it was given freely and willingly — so no one should do injustice to himself. One day all will appear before Allah and answer for their deeds, so no one should sway from the path of righteousness after the Prophet (peace be upon him) is gone.

The Final Message

"O people, no prophet or messenger will come after me, and no new faith will be born. Reason well, therefore, O people, and understand the words which I convey to you. I leave behind me two things, the Quran and my example (the Sunnah), and if you follow these, you will never go astray." All who listen must pass the words on to others, and those to others again; and the last ones may understand the words better than those who listen directly. The sermon ends: "Be my witness, O Allah, that I have conveyed Your message to Your people."

Key Points

  • The Last Address was delivered at Arafat during the last Hajj (10 A.H. / 632 A.D.) and is a complete charter of human rights and duties.
  • The life and property of every Muslim are a sacred trust; entrusted goods must be returned.
  • Interest (usury) is forbidden and all interest obligations are waived; only the capital may be kept.
  • Women have rights over men just as men have rights over women; wives must be treated with kindness.
  • All mankind is equal — superiority is only by piety and good action; Muslims are one brotherhood.
  • The Prophet (peace be upon him) left behind the Quran and his Sunnah; following them keeps a person from going astray.

lessons.title: Unit 1 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The book's Glossary explains the difficult words of this unit. Learn these words with their meanings and their use in the address.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
sacredHoly; embodying the doctrines of a religion. The life and property of every Muslim are sacred.
attentiveWith careful listening, noticing. "Listen to me attentively."
reckonTo establish by calculation; to settle accounts. Allah will reckon your deeds.
be waivedTo refrain from insisting on or using (a right or claim). All interest obligations shall be waived.
astrayAway from the correct path or direction. Satan cannot lead you astray in big things.
legitimateLegal, lawful. Nothing belonging to a fellow Muslim is legitimate unless given freely.
pietyThe quality of being religious. Superiority is only by piety and good action.

Two more words from the address: usury means interest — money charged for lending money; and a trust is something kept safely for another person, to be returned to its rightful owner.

Key Points

  • Sacred = holy; astray = away from the right path.
  • To waive a claim is to give it up willingly.
  • Piety — being truly religious — is the only ground of superiority in the address.

lessons.title: Unit 1 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 1 teaches the present participle and the past participle — their forms, their spelling rules and their uses.

The Present Participle

The present participle is the form of a verb ending in –ing, used in forming continuous tenses, alone in non-finite clauses, and as an adjective.

  • In continuous tenses: The boy was running very fast. All the students were sailing across the Indus river when we reached there.
  • Alone in non-finite clauses: Who is the boy sitting next to you in class? Akram, waiting outside, was getting more and more annoyed.
  • As an adjective: He has a talking parrot. We caught a lot of fish in running water. Skylark is a singing bird.

Rules for Making the –ing Form

  • For many verbs, simply add –ing: eat – eating, cook – cooking, play – playing.
  • Verbs ending in –e: drop the –e and add –ing: hope – hoping, make – making, write – writing (except verbs ending in –ee and –ie).
  • Verbs ending in –ee: just add –ing: agree – agreeing, flee – fleeing, see – seeing.
  • Verbs ending in –ie: change –ie to –y and add –ing: die – dying, tie – tying, lie – lying.
  • Verbs ending in one vowel + one consonant (except w, x, y): for one-syllable verbs, double the consonant and add –ing: sit – sitting, stop – stopping, run – running.
  • For two-syllable verbs, just add –ing if the first syllable is stressed: answer – answering, offer – offering, listen – listening; but double the consonant if the second syllable is stressed: admit – admitting, prefer – preferring, begin – beginning.

The Past Participle

The past participle is the form of a verb, typically ending in –ed, used in forming perfect and passive tenses and as an adjective. The past participle of irregular verbs is formed in various ways.

  • In perfect tenses: He has just painted the door. She had passed the exams with good marks.
  • In the passive voice: The teachers were rewarded for their best performance. The election will be held after three months.
  • As an adjective: He saw a damaged building in the town. People will never buy broken glasses. Ahmed was frustrated to do the same routine work.

Forming Past Participles

  • Regular verbs: mostly add –ed or –d to the base form: talk – talked (+ed), hope – hoped (+d). For some verbs the consonant is doubled: hop – hopped, dip – dipped.
  • Group 1 — all three forms the same: burst – burst – burst; cost, cut, put, shut.
  • Group 2 — past and past participle the same: bring – brought – brought; catch – caught; find – found; lay – laid; lead – led.
  • Group 3 — the vowel changes i → a → u: begin – began – begun; drink – drank – drunk; shrink – shrank – shrunk; ring – rang – rung; swim – swam – swum.
  • Group 4 — past participle formed by adding –n or –en to the past: beat – beat – beaten; break – broke – broken; speak – spoke – spoken; wear – wore – worn; tear – tore – torn.
  • Group 5 — past participle formed from the present by adding –n, –en or –ne: blow – blew – blown; do – did – done; draw – drew – drawn; eat – ate – eaten; see – saw – seen; take – took – taken.

The unit's activity asks you to tick the correct participle: My brother was amused (not amusing) by the comedian; This story is so boring; This Mathematics problem is so confusing; The plane began to move in a rather alarming way; He bought a broken watch. Remember: the –ing form describes the thing that causes the feeling, and the –ed form describes the person who feels it.

Key Points

  • The present participle ends in –ing; the past participle usually ends in –ed.
  • Both participles work in tenses, in the passive voice, and as adjectives.
  • Drop –e before –ing (make – making); change –ie to –y (die – dying); double a final consonant after one short vowel (stop – stopping).
  • Irregular past participles fall into five groups — learn each verb's three forms together.

chapters.title: Unit 2: The Caliph and the Gardener (James Baldwin)

lessons.title: The Caliph and the Gardener — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
The Caliph and the Gardener is a story of honesty and kindness. There was once a caliph of Cordova whose name was Al-Mansur. One day a strange merchant came to him with diamonds and pearls brought from beyond the sea. The caliph was so pleased with the jewels that he bought them and paid the merchant a large sum of money.

The Merchant Loses His Money

The merchant put the gold in a bag of purple silk, tied it to his belt underneath his long cloak, and set out on foot to another city. It was midsummer and very hot. Walking along, he came to a river that flowed gently between green and shady banks. He took off his clothes, laid the bag of money on top of them, and leaped into the refreshing water. Suddenly he heard a rustling noise behind him and saw an eagle rising into the air with his moneybag in its claws — the bird had mistaken the purple silk for something good to eat. The merchant shouted in vain; the great bird flew towards the far-off mountains with all his money, and the poor man dressed himself and went sorrowing on his way.

The Caliph's Clever Plan

A year passed. The merchant appeared once more before Al-Mansur with a few jewels he had reserved as a present for his wife, forced by bad luck to sell them. The caliph noticed that he was very sad and downcast and asked what had happened. Hearing the story, he asked: "Why didn't you come to us before? We might have done something to help you. Toward what place was the eagle flying?" — "It was flying toward the Black Mountains." The next morning the caliph called ten of his officers: "Ride at once to the Black Mountains. Find all the old men that live on the mountains or in the flat country around, and command them to appear before me one week from today."

The Gardener Is Found

On the day appointed, forty grey-bearded, honest old men stood before the caliph. All were asked the same question: "Do you know of any person who was once poor but who has lately and suddenly become well-to-do?" A few said there was one man in their neighbourhood who seemed to have had some sort of good luck — a gardener. A year ago he was so poor that he had scarcely clothes for his back and his children were crying for food, but lately everything had changed: he and his family dressed well, they had plenty to eat, and he had even bought a horse to carry his produce to market. The caliph ordered the gardener and the merchant to be brought before him the next day.

The Gardener's Honest Confession

As soon as the gardener entered the hall, the caliph asked him: "Good friend, if you should find something that we have lost, what would you do with it?" The gardener put his hand under his cloak and drew out the very bag the merchant had lost: "Here it is, my lord." The merchant began to dance and shout with joy. The gardener then told his story: a year ago, spading in his garden, he saw something falling at the foot of a palm tree — a bag full of bright gold pieces. He had thought the money must belong to Al-Mansur, stolen from the palace by some large bird. But looking at the gold, he thought of his own great necessities: his wife and children were suffering from want of food and clothing; he had no shoes for his feet and no coat for his back. Trusting that Al-Mansur, famous for kindness to the poor, would not care, he took ten gold pieces from the bag. "I meant only to borrow them," he said. He had hidden the bag safely, meaning to return it all as soon as he could replace the ten pieces — but with much hard labour he had saved only five little silver pieces. Coming to the palace, he kept telling himself that when the caliph learned how he had borrowed the gold, he would surely forgive the debt.

The Reward of Honesty

Great was the caliph's surprise at the poor man's story. He handed the bag to the merchant: "Take the bag and count the money that is in it. If anything is lacking, I will pay it to you." The merchant counted and said there was nothing lacking but the ten pieces the gardener had told about — and offered those to the gardener as a reward. "No," said Al-Mansur, "it is for me to reward the man as he deserves." He ordered ten gold pieces to be given to the merchant in place of those that were lacking, and rewarded the gardener with ten more pieces for his honesty, saying: "Your debt is paid. Think no more about it."

Note on the author: the book's author box describes James Baldwin (1924–1987), the American novelist. This story, however, is an old tale of the Caliph Al-Mansur retold in simple English — the "About the Author" box does not match the story's origin, so learn the story itself and treat the author box with care.

Key Points

  • An eagle carries away the merchant's bag of gold, mistaking the purple silk for food.
  • The caliph questions forty old men of the Black Mountains and finds the gardener who suddenly became well-to-do.
  • The gardener honestly confesses that he borrowed ten gold pieces in his poverty, intending to repay them.
  • The caliph repays the merchant's ten pieces and gives the gardener ten more as a reward for honesty.
  • The theme of the story is that honesty is always rewarded, and kindness wins hearts.

lessons.title: Unit 2 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The book's Glossary explains the difficult words of this story. Learn these words with their meanings and their use in the story.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
merchantA person or company involved in wholesale trade — one who buys and sells goods. The merchant sold diamonds and pearls to the caliph.
cloakAn over-garment that hangs loosely from the shoulders. The merchant tied the bag under his long cloak.
rustlingMaking a soft, crackling sound like that caused by the movement of dry leaves. The merchant heard a rustling noise behind him.
downcastLooking downwards; sad. The caliph noticed the merchant was sad and downcast.
necessitiesThe state or fact of being required; great needs. The gardener thought of his own great necessities — food and clothing for his family.

Two more words from the story: to go sorrowing is to go along full of sorrow or grief; and well-to-do means rich or prosperous — the gardener had suddenly become well-to-do.

Key Points

  • A merchant trades in goods; a cloak is a loose over-garment.
  • Rustling is a soft crackling sound; downcast means sad, with eyes looking down.
  • Necessities are the things a person cannot live without.

lessons.title: Unit 2 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 2 teaches the perfect participle, and also explains the elements of a story.

The Perfect Participle

The perfect participle indicates a completed action. It is formed by putting the present participle "having" before the past participle: having + past participle. It shows that one action was finished before another action began.

  • Having completed his homework, Ahmed went to attend the debate contest.
  • Having improved her English language, Saima qualified for a job.
  • Having delivered the message, Hassan left for Karachi.

Rewriting with a Perfect Participle

The book's example: "We switched off the lights before we went to bed" becomes "Having switched off the lights, we went to bed." The same pattern answers the unit's activity:

  • He has worked till late hours, so he is exhausted now. → Having worked till late hours, he is exhausted now.
  • She filled the washing machine and switched it on. → Having filled the washing machine, she switched it on.
  • Maria had travelled from Karachi to Quetta, therefore she overslept in the morning. → Having travelled from Karachi to Quetta, Maria overslept in the morning.
  • Since I had not seen Ali for ages, I did not recognize him. → Having not seen Ali for ages, I did not recognize him.
  • Saleem had not ridden a horse for a long time, and found it very difficult to keep in the saddle. → Having not ridden a horse for a long time, Saleem found it very difficult to keep in the saddle.

Elements of a Story

  • Characters — the people or animals in the story.
  • Events — the incidents or happenings in the story.
  • Setting — the time and place of the story.
  • Plot — what happens in the story: Beginning → Middle → End.
  • Theme — the lesson or message of the story.
  • Tone — the writer's attitude (way of thinking and feeling) towards the subject and characters.
  • Point of view — the characters' opinions and beliefs, likes and dislikes.

Key Points

  • The perfect participle = having + past participle, and it shows a completed action before another action.
  • Use it to join two sentences when the same person does both actions, one after the other.
  • Every story has characters, events, setting, plot, theme, tone and point of view.

lessons.title: Patriotism — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Patriotism, by Prof. Abdul Majeed Khan, explains what true love of one's country means — and how it differs from blind, destructive patriotism. Having or expressing love for one's country is what we call patriotism; in other words it means devotion, loyalty and commitment to one's country. It is a noble sentiment which is essential for the integrity and solidarity of a country. A man who lacks this sentiment is nothing short of a dead soul.

Patriotism Is Loyalty to an Ideology

Patriotism is not a mere love for an area of land; it is the ideology of the people living in that land, and patriotism is loyalty to that ideology. True patriotism is not confined to the defence of the country — it also shows its strength in peace time. Patriotism provokes the people to do something great for the country; it motivates them to offer sacrifices for her, and spurs them to make concerted efforts for the progress and prosperity of their country.

What Patriotism Develops in a Patriot

Patriotism inspires a man to contribute to the country. It develops in him a sense of brotherhood, cooperation and sympathy for the countrymen. A patriot feels proud of his country and countrymen. However, a true patriot should never hate other countries, because true patriotism teaches us to love and respect other countries as well. Patriotism is a spirit which arouses the passion of love, unity and a sense of cooperation among the people, which in turn makes them a dynamic force that can push the ship of their country through any tempest or typhoon.

Love of the Motherland Is Natural

The love for one's land is just one aspect of patriotism. A child born in a certain land is liable to develop love for it, no matter how much it is barren of greenery. Patriotism is a natural instinct which compels a man to lay down his life for his country. George Bernard Shaw says, "Patriotism is your conviction that this country is superior to all other countries because you were born in it." That is why we instinctively love our motherland the most in comparison to the rest of the world.

Vicious (Blind) Patriotism

There is a type of patriotism which we may call destructive or blind patriotism. Oscar Wilde says, "Patriotism is the virtue of the vicious." We know how the fascist regime of vicious Hitler exploited the passion of patriotism of the German nation for the destruction of the world. Vicious patriotism is against the teachings of Islam. Islam emphasizes the equality of all human beings: Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) said, "No Arab is superior to a Non-Arab and no Non-Arab is superior to an Arab. No white man is superior to a black man and no black man is superior to a white man. All the human beings are the off-springs of Adam, and Adam was created out of clay." These sayings clearly propound the theory of international brotherhood and negate the philosophy of narrow nationalism based on the superiority of one nation over others on the basis of colour, race or any other consideration. Henry Emerson Fosdick condemned vicious patriotism in these words: "He is a poor patriot whose patriotism does not enable him to understand how all men everywhere feel about their altars and their hearth stones, their flag and their fatherland."

The True Patriot

Buddha has also said in this regard, "To him in whom love dwells, the whole world is but one family." True patriotism is one of the noblest virtues. A true patriot is the one who loves other nations as well, loves to develop friendship with them, and hates the idea of war. However, if any vicious force invades his country, he willingly, rather passionately, defends his country and never hesitates in laying down his life while defending her. A true patriot considers himself the citizen of the world, desirous of peace for the whole world and sensitive to the plight and miseries of other peoples. Ameer Miraal has beautifully explained the virtue of a true patriot in such words: "My heart aches when dagger is pointed at somebody. All the pains of the world are in my heart." The author has taught in the teaching profession since 1981, as JET, SET and Associate Professor, and has translated various textbooks into English.

Key Points

  • Patriotism is devotion, loyalty and commitment to one's country — loyalty to its ideology, not mere love of land.
  • It develops brotherhood, cooperation and sympathy, and inspires sacrifice and service in peace as well as war.
  • Love of the motherland is a natural instinct, as Shaw's words show.
  • Blind or vicious patriotism — believing one's nation superior by race or colour — is condemned by Islam and by thinkers like Fosdick.
  • A true patriot loves all nations, desires peace for the whole world, yet defends his country bravely when it is invaded.

lessons.title: Unit 3 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 3 teaches the infinitive and infinitive phrases, and explains how a thesaurus gives synonyms and antonyms.

The Infinitive

The infinitive is the basic form of a verb, without an inflection binding it to a particular subject or tense, that usually functions as a noun or modifier. Note: the infinitive functions as a noun, an adjective or an adverb — but not as a main verb.

  • As a noun: I want to explain that theory.
  • As an adverb: The inspector came to check the dam.
  • As an adjective: The kind of flowers to plant are tulips.

Infinitive Phrases

An infinitive phrase includes the infinitive plus any modifier and complement. Just like infinitives, infinitive phrases also function like nouns, adjectives or adverbs in a sentence.

  • As a noun: Saima wants to sing a song.
  • As an adverb: Faheem went to buy fruits.
  • As an adjective: Here is a laundry to wash clothes.

The unit's activity gives these infinitives and phrases to use in your own sentences, showing their different functions: to protect, to achieve, to become educated, to vote, to take a walk, to climb, to teach English, to please everyone, to buy groceries, to resign.

Synonyms, Antonyms and the Thesaurus

A thesaurus is a book that contains many synonyms — words that have the same or nearly the same meanings. Entry words in a thesaurus are listed in alphabetical order. Thesauruses generally contain antonyms as well; antonyms are words that have opposite or nearly opposite meanings.

  • Synonyms of happy: cheerful, joyful, blissful.
  • Antonyms of dirty: clean, cleansed, stainless.

Key Points

  • The infinitive is the basic form of a verb (to + verb); it works as a noun, adjective or adverb, never as the main verb.
  • An infinitive phrase = the infinitive + its modifiers and complements, with the same three functions.
  • Synonyms have nearly the same meaning; antonyms have opposite meanings; a thesaurus lists both.

lessons.title: The Spider and the Fly — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
The Spider and the Fly is a famous poem by Mary Howitt (1799–1888), the English poetess, Quaker and reformer. In this poem a cunning spider tries again and again to trap a little fly with sweet, flattering words. The poem is a warning: never listen to flatterers.

Stanza 1: The Invitation to the Parlour

"Will you walk into my parlour?" said the spider to the fly. "It is the prettiest little parlour that ever you did spy. The way into my parlour is up a winding stair, and I have many pretty things to show when you are there." But the little fly refuses: "Oh no, no — to ask me is in vain, for who goes up your winding stair can never come down again."

Stanza 2: The Offer of the Bed

The spider tries again: "I am sure you must be weary, dear, with soaring up so high; will you rest upon my little bed?" There are pretty curtains drawn around, the sheets are fine and thin, and if the fly likes to rest awhile, he will snugly tuck her in. The fly again refuses: "I've often heard it said, they never, never wake again, who sleep upon your bed."

Stanza 3: The Offer of the Pantry

The spider asks what he shall do to prove the warm affection he has always felt for her: "I have within my pantry good store of all that's nice; I am sure you're very welcome — will you please to take a slice?" The fly answers: "Kind Sir, that cannot be; I've heard what's in your pantry, and I do not wish to see."

Stanza 4: Flattery about Her Beauty

Now the spider changes his trick and uses flattery: "Sweet creature! You are witty and you are wise! How handsome are your gauzy wings, how brilliant are your eyes! I have a little looking-glass upon my parlour shelf; if you'll step in one moment, dear, you shall behold yourself." The fly thanks him politely for all he is pleased to say, bids him good morning, and promises to call another day.

Stanza 5: The Spider Prepares the Trap

The spider turned round and went into his den, for he knew well that the silly fly would soon come back again. So he wove a subtle web in a sly little corner and set his table ready to dine upon the fly. Then he came out to his door again and merrily sang: "Come hither, hither, pretty fly, with the pearl and silver wing; your robes are green and purple, there's a crest upon your head; your eyes are like the diamond bright, but mine are dull as lead."

Stanza 6: The Fly Is Trapped

Alas, alas! Very soon this silly little fly, hearing his wily flattering words, came slowly flitting by. With buzzing wings she hung aloft, then near and nearer drew, thinking only of her brilliant eyes and green and purple hue — thinking only of her crested head — poor foolish thing! At last, up jumped the cunning spider and fiercely held her fast. He dragged her up his winding stair, into his dismal den, within his little parlour — but she never came out again.

Stanza 7: The Moral

The poetess now speaks to the readers: "And now, dear little children, who may this story read, to idle, silly, flattering words I pray you never give heed. Unto an evil counsellor close heart, and ear, and eye, and take a lesson from this tale of the Spider and the Fly." People in the world are betrayed and trapped by flattery just as the fly was trapped by the spider.

Key Points

  • The spider invites the fly with three offers — the parlour, the bed and the pantry — and the fly refuses each time.
  • The fly is finally trapped not by the offers but by flattery about her wings, eyes and crested head.
  • The spider stands for evil, flattering people; the fly stands for foolish people who love praise.
  • The moral: close your heart, ear and eye to an evil counsellor and never listen to flattering words.

lessons.title: Unit 4 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 4 teaches the gerund and gerund phrases, and explains genre, personification and alliteration.

The Gerund

A gerund is the –ing form (base form + ing) of a verb that works as a noun. The uses of the gerund are:

  • As a subject: Teaching is a good profession.
  • As an object of verbs and prepositions: He enjoys doing his homework. She was worried about missing her test.
  • As a subject complement: My hobby is reading storybooks. His problem is not coming to office on time.

Gerund Phrases

A gerund phrase is an –ing form of a verb including other modifiers and/or objects, and it functions as a noun.

  • As a subject: Blowing bubbles on a windy day is a great fun for children.
  • As an object of a preposition: The kids were excited about eating birthday cake.
  • As a complement: My ambition is taking part in a debate contest.

The unit's activity gives these gerunds and gerund phrases to use in sentences: taking exams, breathing loudly, parking the car, playing, cooking, helping the needy people, borrowing, taking exercise, going for a morning walk, eating hurriedly.

Genre and Conventions

Genre means a type of art, literature or music characterized by a specific form, content and style — in other words, the different text types. Genres are categorised as fiction (drama, fable, fairytales, short stories, legends, poetry and science fiction) and non-fiction (autobiographies, biographies, essays, informational texts, narrative non-fiction and speech). Conventions are the linguistic and non-linguistic features that identify a certain genre. The important features of a poem are: experiences (the author's life, thoughts and feelings), images (words that make pictures in your mind) and structure (sections called stanzas, which are not always complete sentences).

Personification and Alliteration

Personification is a literary technique in which human qualities or activities are given to an object or animal. It adds interest and fun to a poem or story: in this poem Mary Howitt has mentioned the spider and the fly as if they are talking to each other like human beings. Alliteration is a figure of speech and a stylistic device which occurs when words that start with the same sound are used close together in a phrase or sentence — for example, "Oh, no, no," said the little fly, and "They never, never wake again."

Key Points

  • A gerund is the –ing form of a verb used as a noun; a gerund phrase adds modifiers or objects to it.
  • Gerunds work as subjects, objects and complements — unlike the present participle, which works as an adjective or in continuous tenses.
  • Personification gives human qualities to animals or things; alliteration repeats the same opening sound in nearby words.

lessons.title: The Blanket — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
The Blanket is a touching short story by Floyd Dell (1887–1969), the American writer. The book's introduction says that dealing with old people in modern society has become a serious problem: sometimes they are rejected even by their own relatives, and elderly people are sent to special homes for the aged. The story shows how a little boy's love teaches his father a lesson.

Sending Granddad Away

Petey, a boy of eleven, hadn't really believed that Dad would be doing it — sending Granddad away. "Away" was what they called it: the old man was to go the next morning to the great brick building, the government place (the old house), where he would be with many other old fellows. Dad had bought him a blanket to go away with. Dad himself was out that evening, seeing the girl he was going to marry; he would move into a new house with her. This was the last evening the old man and the little boy would have together.

The Last Evening Together

It was a fine September night, with a silver moon riding high over the valley. After the supper dishes were washed, the old man and the boy went out on the porch of the hut with their chairs. "I'll get my fiddle," said the old man, "and play you some of the old tunes." But instead of the fiddle, he brought out the blanket — a double blanket, red, with black stripes. Smoothing it over his knees, he praised it: "Now isn't that a fine blanket? And isn't your father a kind man to give the old fellow a blanket like that to go away with? It cost something, it did — look at its wool! And it will certainly keep me warm these cold nights to come." He was trying to make it easier for the boy; all along he had pretended that it was he who wanted to go away, to the place where he'd be with so many other old fellows having the best of everything. Petey went into the hut to fetch Granddad's fiddle — he wasn't the kind to cry, and besides he was too old for that, being eleven. Granddad tuned up and played: "This is one you'd like to remember." The silver moon was high overhead and a gentle breeze played down the valley. Petey knew he could never hear Granddad play like this again.

Granddad Makes Excuses for Dad

The tune changed — "Here's something merrier" — but then it stopped suddenly. Granddad said it was a fine girl Dad was going to marry: "He'll feel young again, with a pretty wife like that. And what would an old fellow like me do around the house, getting in the way, an old nuisance, what with my talk of aches and pains! And then there'll be babies coming, and I'd not want to be there to hear them crying all hours. It's best that I take myself off like I'm doing." He played one more tune — "a bit sad, but a fine tune for a night like this."

The Girl Objects to the Double Blanket

They didn't hear the two people coming down the valley path — Dad and the pretty girl, with the hard, bright face like a china doll's. But they heard her laugh, right by the porch, and the tune stopped on a wrong, high, startled note. The girl had come to say goodbye, since she wouldn't see Granddad leave in the morning. Seeing the blanket at his feet, Granddad picked it up and said in embarrassment: "And will you look at this? The fine blanket my son has given me to go away with!" She felt the wool and repeated in surprise, "A fine blanket — I'll say it is!" Then she turned to Dad and said coldly, "It cost something, that." Dad cleared his throat and said defensively, "I wanted him to have the best —" But the girl stood there, still intent on the blanket, and said reproachfully to Dad: "It's double, too." Granddad agreed: "Yes, it's double — a fine blanket for an old fellow to go away with." Hearing the girl criticizing Dad, and Dad becoming angry in his slow way, Petey went into the hut looking for something. As the girl suddenly went away angrily up the valley path, she called out: "All the same, he doesn't need a double blanket!"

Petey's Lesson: Cut the Blanket in Two

Dad looked after her uncertainly. "Oh, she's right," said the boy coldly — and he held out a pair of scissors: "Here, Dad. Cut the blanket in two." Both men stared at the boy, surprised. "Cut it in two, I tell you, Dad!" he cried out. "And keep one half!" Granddad said gently that it wasn't a bad idea — he didn't need so much of a blanket. "Yes," said the boy harshly. "A single blanket's enough for an old man when he's sent away. We'll save the other half, Dad; it will come in handy later." "Now, what do you mean by that?" asked Dad. "I mean," said the boy slowly, "that I'll give it to you, Dad — when you're old and I send you away."

The Ending

There was silence. Then Dad went over to Granddad and stood before him, not speaking. But Granddad understood, for he put out his hand and laid it on Dad's shoulder. Petey heard Granddad whisper: "It's all right, son — I know you didn't mean it." But it didn't matter — because they were all three crying together. Dad changed his decision: Granddad would not be sent away. Petey had taught his Dad the lesson that parents are a blessing, and that what we do to our parents, our children will one day do to us.

Key Points

  • Dad is sending old Granddad to the old house because he is marrying a young girl and moving to a new house.
  • Granddad pretends he wants to go, and praises the fine double blanket Dad bought him, to make it easier for everyone.
  • The girl objects that Granddad does not need a double blanket.
  • Petey asks Dad to cut the blanket in two and save half — for Dad himself, when Petey sends him away in his old age.
  • Dad understands the lesson, is ashamed, and changes his decision; the story's universal theme is the parent–child relationship: treat your parents as you wish to be treated.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning

lessons.title: Unit 5 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 5 teaches adjective phrases and adjective clauses, and how to find the main idea of a paragraph.

Adjective Phrases

An adjective phrase is a group of words that describes a noun or pronoun in a sentence. It can be placed before or after the noun or pronoun.

  • The movie was not too terribly long.
  • A person smarter than me needs to figure this out.
  • The final exams were unbelievably difficult.
  • This pie is very delicious and extremely expensive.
  • Everyone was extremely delighted when the winner was announced.

In the unit's activity, the adjective phrases are: Faster than a speeding bullet (Superman was finished in no time); upset about the rising cost of tuition (students staged a rally); quite small but cheap (that complex has apartments); highly emotive (the actor gave a wonderful performance); not very healthy (eating out); extremely tired (the kitten fell asleep); covered in mud (a dog makes a mess in a car); riding into the sunset (cowboys were in the final scenes); covered in sweat (the man took a break); annoyingly loud (the music from next door).

Adjective Clauses

An adjective clause is a dependent clause that, like an adjective, modifies a noun or pronoun. Adjective clauses begin with words such as that, when, where, who, whom, whose, which and why. An essential (restrictive) adjective clause provides information that is necessary for identifying the word it modifies. A nonessential (nonrestrictive) adjective clause provides additional information about the word it modifies, but the word's meaning is already clear; nonessential clauses are always set off with commas. Note: use that for essential clauses and which for nonessential clauses.

  • Essential: The art class that Samina takes focuses on design. (The clause has a subject, Samina, and a verb, takes; it modifies the noun class.)
  • We are going to the beach that I like the best. (modifies beach)
  • Mr. Naseem is the teacher who helped me with my math problems. (modifies teacher)
  • The bad weather is the reason why I decided to drive instead of walk. (modifies reason)
  • Maria is the person whose family owns a horse ranch. (modifies person)
  • This is the park where we can walk in the evening. (modifies park)
  • Do you remember the time when we almost missed the train? (modifies time)
  • Nonessential: The house on the left, which belongs to Javed, is up for sale. Hameed, who teaches English language, is my best friend. Quetta, which is capital of Balochistan, is a small city. Tiger, which runs very fast, is a dangerous animal.

Main Idea and Supporting Details

The main idea of a paragraph or a longer reading is the most important thing that the writer wants the readers to understand — in an essay it is carried in the thesis statement. Supporting details are pieces of information that show that the main idea is true. The book's example: "The weather outside was terrible" (main idea) — "The temperature was –10°C; the wind was blowing very hard and it was snowing; I did not want to go out" (supporting details). The main idea is often found in the first or last sentence of a paragraph. The unit also names universal themes — ideas that apply to anyone regardless of cultural differences or geographic location, such as abuse of power, corruption, freedom, and the parent–child relationship (the theme of "The Blanket").

Key Points

  • An adjective phrase describes a noun or pronoun but has no subject–verb pair; an adjective clause has its own subject and verb.
  • Essential clauses identify the noun and take no commas (use that); nonessential clauses add extra information, are set off by commas, and use which.
  • The main idea is the writer's most important point; supporting details prove it.

chapters.title: Unit 6: Dignity of Labour (Prof. Abdul Majeed Khan)

lessons.title: Dignity of Labour — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Dignity of Labour, by Prof. Abdul Majeed Khan, teaches that every honest work is honourable. Life without work is worthless, meaningless, dull and boring; it is work that fills life with joys and happiness. But not every sort of activity deserves to be called work — only that activity which is productive and beneficial for an individual or a society. The work of a sweeper is as sacred and noble as that of a bureaucrat or a doctor.

Work Keeps a Man Happy and Healthy

A busy man remains happy and healthy, whereas an idle person is always gloomy and sick. That is why even the richest men do some sort of work to avoid boredom — it is idleness that eats into the very soul of a man. Work makes a man an optimist and develops in him confidence and pride.

No Profession Is Low

There is no disrespect attached to any profession. A person who tills the land, works in a coal mine or factory, or builds houses is as honourable as the president of a country. Our beloved Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) drove sheep in the pasture, drew water from the well, mended his shoes and did various sorts of menial work, though he is the cause of the creation of the whole universe and the most beloved person of Allah Almighty.

Choose Work According to Your Nature

It is quite necessary for a man to choose such a profession as is compatible with his nature and likings, otherwise he will get fed up with it. It would be wise to have a high purpose. The dignity of labour is now recognized all over the world. If the workers come to realize the dignity and importance of labour, they will feel confident and never fall prey to an inferiority complex. They require to develop a strong conviction of the value of work; only then will they be able to wield the sceptre of power in the world. Workers must be convinced that no work is inferior to another work — the distinction made between one work and another is purely man-made. If there is nobody to sweep our streets or manage our sewerage system, the whole city will turn into a heap of garbage, which will cause the spread of diseases. If the tillers of land refuse to grow wheat and vegetables, we shall definitely starve to death. If the factories stop working, we shall have no clothes to wear and no shoes to put on.

Life Is Action, Not Contemplation

It is quite true that life is action and not contemplation. Man's life is only determined by his actions. It is not enough to know; to act according to knowledge is the main purpose of life. However much knowledge a person may have, unless he applies it in solving the world's problems, he is good for nothing — a sweeper, in comparison with him, is a far more dignified person. If Sir Syed Ahmed Khan has become immortal, it is just because of his great services to his nation.

Work for the Love of Work

A worker should work for the love of work and not for money. It is necessary for him to take joy in doing his work; he must put his soul and heart into his work. Constructive work provides us with joys and happiness. Work is the blessing of Allah Almighty; according to Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him), the hands of a labourer are dear to Allah Almighty. In the words of a great scholar: "Allah is there where the tiller of land is tilling the soil and the path-maker is breaking the stones." The Holy Quran says, "Verily, we have created man in toil."

Nations Rise by Hard Work

Life is the name of continuous struggle and hard work. If we look into the causes of the rise and fall of nations, we shall conclude that it was the efforts and hard struggle of nations which took them to the height of glory, and when they became lethargic and lazy, they met their final doom. Quaid-e-Azam has rightly pointed out the importance of work in his famous saying, "Work, Work and Work" — a sort of advice and a philosophical point containing profound wisdom, which indirectly points out the method of achieving glory in the comity of nations.

Key Points

  • Only productive and beneficial activity is true work; a sweeper's work is as noble as a doctor's or a bureaucrat's.
  • Work keeps a man happy, healthy, confident and proud; idleness eats into the soul.
  • No profession is inferior — the distinction between works is purely man-made, and every worker is needed by society.
  • Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) himself did menial work; the hands of a labourer are dear to Allah.
  • Life is action, not contemplation; nations rise by hard work and fall by laziness — "Work, Work and Work."

lessons.title: Unit 6 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 6 teaches the use of all the tenses, and how to tell a fact from an opinion.

Fact and Opinion

A fact is something that can be proven. An opinion is a belief that may be true but cannot be proven. The book's examples: "There are five rooms in our school" is a fact; "Our school is very beautiful" is an opinion.

The Simple Tenses

  • Present Simple — repeated actions in the present (He drinks milk daily); actions that happen in general (The Sun rises in the East); set events of the near future (We go to Karachi next week); current facts (If we mix red and green, we get yellow).
  • Past Simple — completed actions in the past (He passed his test yesterday); a duration of time in the past (She always carried an umbrella).
  • Future Simple — a specific action in the future (Ali will go to Khuzdar tomorrow); a promise (I will pay you ten thousand rupees); a plan (We will stay at Pishin); a prediction (It will rain in the next month).

The Perfect Tenses

  • Present Perfect — actions at an unspecific time in the past (Ahmed has travelled overseas several times); actions that started in the past and continue to the present (The children have felt sick ever since they ate lunch); past experiences (We have eaten at that restaurant once or twice).
  • Past Perfect — an action that happened before another action in the past (The aeroplane had taken off before they reached the airport); duration before something that finished in the past (I met him in Dubai in 1980; I had seen him last five years before).
  • Future Perfect — a completed action happening before something in the future (They will have left for Chaman before you go to see them); duration before something in the future (I will have written the essay by that time).

The Continuous Tenses

  • Present Continuous — an action happening (or not happening) now (I am reading a novel now); an action currently in progress (I am learning English); a planned future action (They are going to Islamabad tomorrow).
  • Past Continuous — an action going on at some time in the past (When I saw him, he was playing tennis); persistent habits in the past (He was always speaking loudly).
  • Future Continuous — an action going on at some time in the future (When I get home, my children will be doing their homework).
  • Present Perfect Continuous — events which started in the past and are still continuing (Umer has been living next door to me for two years).
  • Past Perfect Continuous — an ongoing action that started in the past and continued for some time in the past (He had been teaching English for ten years before he retired).
  • Future Perfect Continuous — an ongoing action that will complete in the future (She will have been serving as a social worker for two years when we leave the city).

Key Points

  • Simple tenses show completed or habitual actions; perfect tenses link one time with another; continuous tenses show actions in progress.
  • The perfect continuous tenses show how long an action has been, had been, or will have been going on.
  • A fact can be proven; an opinion is a belief that cannot be proven.

chapters.title: Unit 7: The Choice of a Career (Prof. Abdul Majeed Khan)

lessons.title: The Choice of a Career — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
The Choice of a Career, by Prof. Abdul Majeed Khan, guides the youth on choosing the right profession. The prosperity and bright future of a man depends largely on the profession that he chooses. The right choice of a career leads to a happy and healthy life, whereas the wrong one leads to a gloomy and sad one. It is therefore imperative for a young man to carefully choose his career, taking into account all the pros and cons of it, making sure that it suits his tastes and talents. Besides, he should consider the future of that career and not drift along the current.

Choose with Utmost Care

We should choose our profession with utmost care, for arbitrary decisions often lead to despair and ruin. In the past, the youths followed the professions of their parents; they needed not bother themselves with the thoughts of choosing any profession. A merchant's son would become a merchant and a cobbler's son a cobbler. But now the social conditions have completely changed. The culture of democracy has changed the mindset and outlook of the people. Today every individual tends to choose a profession of his own choice. However, choosing a suitable career that could guarantee a respectable position in society is not that easy. It requires clear vision and far-sightedness, which is not so common among the youth. It is therefore necessary for them to consult their elders and specialists before making a decision, and to keep themselves abreast of the new trends not only in their society but in the whole world.

Match Taste and Talent — but Remember Money

A young man should not just consider the material benefits that a career may provide; he should also see if his tastes and talents match it. It doesn't mean that he should totally ignore the financial aspect of his career: a person cannot live through life by holding on to his taste alone; he has to earn a reasonable amount of money to lead a decent life. For example, a young boy who has a talent and taste for music or sculpture and decides to become a professional musician or sculptor is likely to repent later and get frustrated when he fails to earn his living through these careers. He may choose such things as a hobby, for there are many cases of such professionals becoming penniless and destitute in the end; only a fraction of them become popular and successful. Thus a youth must not put at stake his future on such a career in which the chances of success are little.

Once Chosen, Persevere

But once the choice is made, one should put one's heart into it. He might get bored at times while performing his duties, and even lose heart, but he has to curb the feelings of despair that arise in his mind and devote himself to his profession. He must face courageously the difficulties that come in his way and must not lose heart. There are some fickle-minded people who shift from profession to profession; such rolling stones never achieve success in their life. Perseverance is the key to success, and tenacity of purpose eventually bears the fruit. Many people started their career in very unfavourable circumstances, yet achieved their goals by sheer dint of hard work and strong will. Abraham Lincoln, the son of a poor farmer, chose to become a lawyer and put his whole-hearted efforts into the profession; gradually he became popular among the masses and was eventually elected President of the United States of America. Quaid-e-Azam was the son of a merchant; he chose the same profession of law, then entered the arena of politics and devoted himself to the welfare of the Muslim nation. He was elected President of the All-India Muslim League; later he demanded a separate homeland for the Indian Muslims and succeeded in carving out a new country, Pakistan, on the world map. His devotion to his profession and dedication to his cause won him the title of "Father of the Nation".

The Problem in Pakistan

In our country, Pakistan, the literacy rate is too low, and thus the majority of the people are conservative and orthodox. The youth are not allowed to choose the career of their own choice; the parents force their wards to adopt their family professions. Thus the clash of interest between the parents and their wards results in either poor performance or complete failure. Such wards tend to think of themselves as a square peg in a round hole. Besides, there are limited opportunities for our youth in most professions. Most of our young men wish to choose professions like medicine, engineering or law, whereas the brilliant ones try their luck in the C.S.S. (Central Superior Services). However, these are already overcrowded, and only a fraction of them succeed. A large number of young men wander about in search of jobs; the majority of them get jobs of clerks or small-rank officials — so our educational institutions are churning out a race of clerks.

Technical Education — the Way Forward

A German scholar was once asked about the reason of the development of their country. He replied that the progress and development of his country lay in establishing technical training centres in which the young men were trained in various trades and crafts. The same is the reason of the development of other European countries. In Pakistan there are only a few technical training centres, and even these are not properly equipped with modern technology; that is why we lack skilled workers in every field and could not make progress in technology or industry. Fortunately, the present government has realized the need to establish technical institutions: in recent years technical education has been introduced in many colleges and many technical institutes have been established. Thanks to the role of media, especially the electronic one, our young generation is gradually developing an outward-looking approach and dynamism which the old generation was lacking. Now they want to become engineers, scientists and economists; they are no more interested in office jobs; today they are inclined towards joining the Army, Navy and Air Force. This change of outlook in the youth augurs well for the future of our country: we can hope that our country will become as developed and prosperous as the European countries.

Key Points

  • The right career, matched to one's tastes and talents, leads to a happy life; a wrong or arbitrary choice leads to despair.
  • Consult elders and specialists, and consider both your interest and the money a career can earn.
  • Once the choice is made, persevere — rolling stones never succeed; Lincoln and Quaid-e-Azam rose by hard work and devotion.
  • In Pakistan, parents forcing family professions make the youth feel like a square peg in a round hole.
  • Technical training centres made Germany and Europe developed; Pakistan needs more of them, properly equipped.

lessons.title: Unit 7 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 7 teaches adverbs, adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses.

Adverbs

A word that modifies the meaning of an adjective, a verb or another adverb in a sentence is called an adverb.

  • Ahmed is financially weak. (modifies the adjective weak)
  • The weather is terribly hot today.
  • We should drive very carefully. (modifies the verb drive)
  • He plays tennis extremely well. (modifies the adverb well)

Adverbial Phrases

A group of words that describes the action of a verb is called an adverbial phrase.

  • Are you sitting in a comfortable chair?
  • He draws cartoons like a real cartoonist.
  • The train arrived on time.

Adverbial Clauses

A subordinate clause that usually describes the action of a verb is called an adverbial clause. There are different kinds of adverbial clauses:

  • Of manner — tells how an action happens: A crow attacked a cat while I was waiting for the bus. The dog is walking around like he owns the place. He is behaving as if he were our boss.
  • Of place — tells where an action takes place: Put the sign where the students can read it. She can study wherever she wants. He stayed where it was comfortable.
  • Of time — tells when an action takes place: Every time he cracked a joke, the punters roared with laughter. When the train arrived, they had left the station.
  • Of degree — tells to what extent an action takes place: He is not as intelligent as he thinks he is. He is as modest as he is brilliant.
  • Of reason — tells the reason of an action: He came late because his car got out of order. Since he is working hard, he can win the contest.
  • Of condition — tells the condition for a certain result: If they have enough money, they will arrange a nice party. I will help you provided that you become a good person.
  • Of concession — expresses an idea that suggests the opposite of the main part of the sentence: Though he is poor, he is honest. Even if I fail, I will contest once again.

Key Points

  • An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb.
  • An adverbial phrase has no subject–verb pair; an adverbial clause has its own subject and verb.
  • Adverbial clauses answer: how (manner), where (place), when (time), how much (degree), why (reason), on what condition, and despite what (concession).

lessons.title: Be the Best of Whatever You Are — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
Be the Best of Whatever You Are is an encouraging poem by Douglas Malloch (1877–1938), the American poet known as the "Lumberman's Poet". The poem teaches one simple lesson: whatever work or place you have in life, big or small, do it in the best possible way. Success does not depend on size, but on doing your own task well.

Stanza 1: Be the Best Little Scrub

"If you can't be a pine on the top of the hill, be a scrub in the valley — but be the best little scrub by the side of the rill; be a bush if you can't be a tree." The pine is a tall tree that stands proudly on the hilltop; the scrub is a small bush in the valley. If you cannot hold a high position, hold your small position in the best way. "If you can't be a bush, be a bit of the grass, and some highway happier make" — even a little grass can make a roadside pleasant. "If you can't be a muskie, then just be a bass — but the liveliest bass in the lake!" The muskie is a big fish and the bass a smaller one; be the most active and best of your own kind.

Stanza 2: Captains and Crew

"We can't all be captains, we've got to be crew; there's something for all of us here. There's big work to do, and there's lesser to do, and the task we must do is the near." A ship needs both a captain and a crew. Every person has some work to do in the world — some big, some small — and our duty is the work that is nearest to us, the work given to us.

Stanza 3: Highway, Trail, Sun and Star

"If you can't be a highway, then just be a trail; if you can't be the sun, be a star. It isn't by size that you win or you fail — be the best of whatever you are!" A highway is a great road and a trail is a small path; the sun is the greatest light and a star is a small one. Winning and failing do not depend on how big your position is, but on how well you perform in it.

The Theme of the Poem

The main theme of the poem is that everyone should perform his or her duty well at his own place. No work is small if it is done in the best way. The poet uses pictures from nature — pine and scrub, muskie and bass, sun and star — as metaphors for high and low positions in life, and tells us to be the best at our own place instead of feeling sad about not holding a high place.

Key Points

  • The poem's message: be the best of whatever you are — do your own duty in the best way.
  • Pine/scrub, muskie/bass, highway/trail and sun/star stand for big and small positions in life.
  • We cannot all be captains; the crew is just as necessary, and the task we must do is the one near us.
  • It is not size that decides success or failure, but the quality of our work.

lessons.title: Unit 8 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 8 teaches nouns, noun phrases and noun clauses — including their use in apposition — and the figurative language of poems.

Figurative Language: Simile, Metaphor, Imagery

Writers and poets use figurative language to appeal to the senses and make their stories and poems more interesting. A simile is a comparison using the words "like" or "as": He ran like wind; She is as beautiful as a rose. A metaphor describes something by comparing it to something else, without "like" or "as": Qasim has a heart of stone; He is a lion. Imagery is figurative language which creates mental images, figures or pictures through descriptive language; it improves the reader's experience through the five senses — as the poem pictures the pine on the hill and the scrub by the rill.

Nouns and Their Uses

A noun is a word that functions as the name of something or a set of things, such as living creatures, objects, places, actions, qualities, states of existence or ideas: The cat sat on the mat; They studied in school for ten years; Cleanliness is half the faith; The man who controls anger is a strong man. In a sentence, nouns can play the role of subject, object, complement or appositive.

  • As subject: Ahmed is an intelligent student. My friend secured an A+ grade in M.Phil.
  • As object: I gave many books (direct object) to my friend (indirect object).
  • As complement: He is a very good teacher. They appointed him as a lecturer.
  • As appositive: My brother, Ali, is 25 years old. ("Ali" immediately follows another noun to further define it.)

Noun Phrases

A noun phrase is a phrase that has a noun as its head and can occupy the same slot as a single noun in a sentence: I am afraid of spiders (noun) — I am afraid of black spiders (noun phrase); She was reading a book — She was reading her favourite book. Uses of noun phrases:

  • As subject: A boy with short hair was standing outside the departmental store. The books on the shelf belong to my brother.
  • As object: He was talking to a boy with short hair. He ordered for the books on the shelf.
  • As complement: This room is the guest room. This is a two litre bottle.
  • In apposition: two noun phrases are put together to refer to the same person or thing — The bookshelf, a modern piece of furniture, was moved into the house first. The insect, a large and hairy creature, scared the children.

Noun Clauses

A noun clause is a subordinate clause that can have the same function, or fill the same slot in a sentence, as a noun.

  • As subject: Whoever ate my lunch is in big trouble. That the department cancelled the lecture disappoints me.
  • As object: Do you know when the train will arrive? I do not know who he was talking to.
  • As complement: The truth is that he secured an A+ grade. The committee has announced the winner, whoever wrote the essay on noun clauses.
  • In apposition: That man, whoever he is, bought some books to read. The problem, that the earthquake demolished the town, affected his senses.

Key Points

  • A simile uses "like" or "as"; a metaphor compares directly; imagery paints pictures for the senses.
  • Nouns, noun phrases and noun clauses can all work as subject, object, complement or appositive.
  • Apposition means placing a noun, phrase or clause next to another to define it further.

lessons.title: The Scholarship Jacket — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
The Scholarship Jacket is a short story by Marta Salinas (born 1949), told by the narrator Martha in the first person. To filter through is to pass or become known slowly, a little at a time — during those two weeks, only a word here and there filtered through to Martha. It is a personal narrative — a story about real events that happened to the author. The small Texas school that Martha attended carried out a tradition every year during the eighth-grade graduation: a beautiful gold and green jacket — the school colours — was awarded to the class valedictorian, the student who had maintained the highest grades for eight years. The scholarship jacket had a big gold S on the left front side, and the winner's name was written in gold letters on the pocket.

Martha's Hope

Martha's oldest sister Rosie had won the jacket a few years back, and Martha fully expected to win it too. She was fourteen and in the eighth grade; she had been a straight-A student since the first grade, and for the last year she had looked forward to owning that jacket. Her father was a farm labourer who couldn't earn enough money to feed eight children, so when she was six she was given to her grandparents to raise. The children couldn't participate in sports at school because there were registration fees, uniform costs and trips out of town; so even though they were quite agile and athletic, there would never be a sports jacket for them. This one, the scholarship jacket, was their only chance.

The Argument She Overhears

In May, close to graduation, Martha had forgotten her P.E. shorts in a bag under her desk and had to walk back to her classroom to get them. Coach Thompson was a real bear if anyone wasn't dressed for P.E., and she had once tried to talk Grandma into letting Martha join the team — Grandma, of course, said no. Almost back at her classroom door, Martha heard angry voices arguing. She didn't mean to eavesdrop; she just hesitated. The voices were Mr. Schmidt, her history teacher, and Mr. Boone, her math teacher — and they were arguing about her. Mr. Schmidt was very angry: "I refuse to do it! I don't care who her father is, her grades don't even begin to compare to Martha's. I won't lie or falsify records. Martha has a straight A-plus average and you know it!" Mr. Boone's voice was calm and quiet: "Look, Joann's father is not only on the Board, he owns the only store in town; we could say it was a close tie and —" The pounding in Martha's ears drowned out the rest; only a few words filtered through: "…Martha is Mexican… resign… won't do it…" Mr. Schmidt came rushing out toward the auditorium, so he didn't see her. Shaking, Martha grabbed her bag and fled. She went home very sad and cried into her pillow that night so her grandmother wouldn't hear her.

The Principal Announces a New Policy

The next day the principal called her into his office. He looked uncomfortable and unhappy; she decided she wasn't going to make it any easier for him, so she looked him straight in the eye while he fidgeted with the papers on his desk. "Martha," he said, "there's been a change in policy this year regarding the scholarship jacket. As you know, it has always been free. This year the Board decided to charge fifteen dollars — which still won't cover the complete cost of the jacket." Then he added: "So if you are unable to pay the fifteen dollars for the jacket, it will be given to the next one in line." Martha stared at him in shock. Standing with all the dignity she could muster, she said: "I'll speak to my grandfather about it, sir, and let you know tomorrow." She cried on the walk home from the bus stop; by the time she got home her eyes were red and puffy. The jacket meant more than being valedictorian and giving a little thank-you speech on graduation night — it represented eight years of hard work and expectation, and she knew she had to be honest with Grandpa; it was her only chance.

Grandpa Refuses to Pay

Grandpa was out back working in the bean field, walking between the rows, his body bent over the little plants, hoe in hand. Martha spoke to him in Spanish, the only language he knew: "Grandpa, this year the principal said the scholarship jacket is not going to be free. It's going to cost fifteen dollars, and I have to take the money in tomorrow; otherwise it'll be given to someone else." Grandpa straightened up tiredly and leaned his chin on the hoe handle. He looked out over the field filled with tiny green bean plants, and then asked quietly: "What does a scholarship jacket mean?" Martha answered quickly: "It means you've earned it by having the highest grades for eight years, and that's why they're giving it to you." Too late, she realized the significance of her words. Grandpa went back to hoeing the weeds, and finally he spoke again: "Then if you pay for it, Martha, it's not a scholarship jacket, is it? Tell your principal I will not pay the fifteen dollars."

Martha Delivers the Message

Martha locked herself in the bathroom for a long time. She was angry with her grandfather, even though she knew he was right, and angry with the Board: why did they have to change the rules just when it was her turn to win the jacket? The next day a very sad and withdrawn girl dragged herself into the principal's office. This time he did look her in the eyes. "What did your grandfather say?" She sat very straight in her chair: "He said to tell you he won't pay the fifteen dollars." The principal muttered something under his breath and walked over to the window. "Why?" he finally asked. "Your grandfather has the money. Doesn't he own a small bean farm?" Martha looked at him, forcing her eyes to stay dry: "He said if I had to pay for it, then it wouldn't be a scholarship jacket." She stood up to leave: "I guess you'll just have to give it to Joann." She hadn't meant to say that; it had just slipped out. She was almost to the door when he stopped her: "Martha — wait."

The Happy Ending

The principal sighed loudly and went back to his big desk. He looked at her, biting his lip as if thinking: "Okay. We'll make an exception in your case. I'll tell the Board — you'll get your jacket." Martha could hardly believe it: "Oh, thank you, sir!" She felt something pumping through her, making her feel as tall as the sky; she wanted to yell, jump, run the mile. She ran out so she could cry in the hall where no one would see her. At the end of the day Mr. Schmidt winked at her and said, "I hear you're getting a scholarship jacket this year." His face looked as happy and innocent as a baby's, but she knew better; without answering, she gave him a quick hug and ran to the bus. She cried on the walk home again — but this time because she was so happy. She ran straight to the field and joined Grandpa in the row where he was working; without saying anything she crouched down and started pulling up the weeds with her hands. After a little pile of weeds stood between the rows, she stood up and faced him: "The principal said he's making an exception for me, Grandpa, and I'm getting the jacket after all. That's after I told him what you said." Grandpa didn't say anything; he just gave her a pat on the shoulder and a smile, pulled out the crumpled red handkerchief he always carried in his back pocket, and wiped the sweat off his forehead. "Better go see if your grandmother needs any help with supper." Martha gave him a big grin — he didn't fool her. She skipped and ran back to the house, whistling some silly tune. The author, Marta Salinas, was born in Coalinga, California, and received a degree in creative writing from the University of California at Irvine; "The Scholarship Jacket" is one of her short stories published in journals and collections.

Key Points

  • The scholarship jacket goes to the valedictorian — the student with the highest grades for eight years — and it had always been free.
  • Martha, a poor Mexican girl raised by her grandparents, has earned it with a straight A-plus average.
  • Mr. Boone wants the jacket given to Joann, whose father is on the Board; Mr. Schmidt refuses to falsify records.
  • The Board's new fifteen-dollar charge is a trick to take the jacket from Martha, who cannot pay.
  • Grandpa refuses on principle: a scholarship that is paid for is not a scholarship.
  • Martha's honesty and her grandfather's principle win: the principal makes an exception and she gets her jacket.

lessons.title: Unit 9 — Grammar Points

Unit 9 teaches prepositions of position, time and movement, and explains the narrator, the author's purpose and transitional words.

The Narrator and the Author's Purpose

The speaker or narrator in a story is the person who tells the story. In "The Scholarship Jacket" the narrator is the author herself, Martha Salinas; she uses the pronouns "I, me, my, we, us, our" — the first-person point of view. When an author writes something, he or she has a purpose: (a) to entertain — the author has a funny or unusual story to tell; (b) to inform — the author tells us about a thing, animal or place to give information; (c) to express an opinion — for example, "Eagles are proud birds"; (d) to persuade — the author wants us to do something. A personal narrative is a story about real events that happened to the author; its features are: characters = real people in the author's life; events and problems = events and problems in the author's life; and the first-person point of view.

Transitional Words

Transitional words are words or groups of words that connect ideas; they help readers follow the chronological order. The book groups them as: Time — in 1977, on Tuesday, in the morning, at noon, ten years ago; Sequence — first, second, next, then, finally; Period of time — for five years, in the summer, last week, for five days, for few moments.

Prepositions: The Three Kinds

A preposition is a word that shows how a noun or a pronoun is related to other words in the sentence. Prepositions show: (1) position — between, among, on, upon, above, over, below, under, etc.; (2) time — in, at, after, later, ago, before, etc.; (3) movement and direction — to, towards, through, into, across, over, along, etc., most often used with verbs of motion, after the verb.

Prepositions of Position

  • Between separates two things; used in the middle of two objects or locations: My office is between my college and home. Among shows belonging to a group; used when comparing with more than two: She is tallest among the three siblings.
  • On — things touching and above something: The cat is on the table. Upon — one thing in motion, the other at rest: The leopard jumped upon the deer.
  • Above — vertically higher, not in contact: The parachute jumper is flying above the clouds. Over — covering, higher: There is a bridge over the river.
  • Below — lower than, not in contact: Questions are given below the text. Under — exactly below, vertically down: My brother is sitting under a tree.
  • Across — the opposite side: There is a mango tree across the river. Through — crossing from within something: He went out through the window.
  • Beside — next to: She is sitting beside the teacher. Near — nearby: His office is near his apartment. Opposite to — the other side: The bank is opposite to the Government College. By — next to: There is a small jug by the bed.
  • In front of — facing something: There is a cupboard in front of my fridge. Behind — at the back: The teacher is standing behind me. At indicates a location or position in time, scale or order; in is used with the larger area: I live in Germany.

Prepositions of Time

  • After / later: use after + phrase; use later alone, at the end of a sentence or phrase (I'll call you later; I'll call you after I get home from work; I'll finish the project later this week). Never end a sentence with "after" — use "afterwards": "No, we went out for drinks afterwards." (Correct)
  • Ago / before: ago refers back from the current moment (He taught English language ten years ago); before refers to a moment in the past (The train had arrived before we reached the station).
  • By / until: by = one specific event before a certain time (Please send me the information by Monday); until = a continuous event that continues and then stops (He's staying in Karachi until the 30th).
  • During / while: both mean at the same time as something else; use during + noun (She cried during the movie); use while + subject + verb, or while + gerund (She cried while she was watching the movie; She cried while watching the movie).
  • From … to / till / until define the beginning and end of a period: The museum is open from 8 AM to 4 PM; I studied English from 2001 till 2004.
  • On / in / at: in for centuries, decades, years, seasons and months (in the 18th century, in 2001, in the summer, in October); on for days (on Friday, on March 15th, on my birthday); at for times (at 3:30, at noon, at quarter past four) — but in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening, at night. Past / to are used with minutes: 3:50 = ten to four; 6:15 = quarter past six.
  • For / since: for = a period of time (I've been waiting for three hours); since = a specific point in time (I've been waiting since ten o'clock). As soon as = immediately after another event (We'll call you as soon as we arrive); as long as = for the period of time, or on the condition that (I stayed awake for as long as I could; I'll take the job as long as I have the freedom to work from home).

Prepositions of Movement

  • To — movement with the aim of a specific destination, a place or an event: I'm travelling to France tomorrow. "Up to" is often used for movement to a person: He came up to me and asked me what the time was. Towards — movement in a particular direction: She was walking towards him.
  • Through — movement within a three-dimensional space, across an entire space from one side to another: They couldn't get the new sofa through the door; He cut through the wire. Into — movement from the outside to the inside: We got into the back of the car.
  • Across / over / along — movement from one side of a place to another, for surfaces (a lawn) or lines (a river): I'll jump over the wall and open the gate; How are we going to get across the stream? Over also expresses position, like above: There was a mirror above/over the sink.
  • In and on: in mainly shows position inside a surrounding space (They were having a picnic in the park), but in can also express movement towards the inside of a container, place or area: Can you put the milk in the fridge?

Key Points

  • Prepositions show position (where), time (when) and movement (where to).
  • Between is for two, among for more than two; on touches, above does not; under is directly below.
  • In + months/years, on + days, at + clock times; for + period, since + point of time.
  • Transitional words (first, next, then, finally) keep the order of events clear.
