lessons.title: Gender Inequality — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Gender Inequality, by Prof. Abdul Majeed Khan, examines the status of women through history and shows that Islam gave women their rights fourteen hundred years ago. Since the inception of civilization, women have been struggling to win recognition of their rights. They have been subjected to discrimination and tyranny ever since, and even today, in this so-called modern era, they are deprived of many rights. Thinkers and philosophers of all ages have expressed various opinions about her status and position in society, and the debate is still going on.

What the Thinkers and Religions Said

Socrates said, "Once made equal to man, woman becomes his superior." According to Edmund Burke, "A woman is but an animal and an animal not of the highest order." Manu, ancient India's law-giver, says: "In childhood must a female be dependent on her father; in youth on her husband; and woman must never seek independence." According to Buddhism, "Nirwana" (salvation), the ultimate goal of human life, cannot be attained in the company of women. The Orthodox Christians consider women as the cause of all evils, for it was Eve that enticed Adam to commit the first sin by eating the forbidden fruit, which caused the Great Fall. In Judaism, Hebrew scriptures condemn women to an eternal curse: "Of the women came the beginning of sin and through her we all die." The picture of women in pre-Islamic Arab society speaks of their pitiable condition: they were considered a disgrace to their families; female children were buried alive; women were treated as the personal property of menfolk; young maidens were traded as slaves in the open markets.

Islam Raised Woman's Status

Islam is the only religion which has made serious efforts to place women at a respectable place in society. It changed the mindset of man, including his social and religious thinking, and gave a vast amount of freedom to women, enabling them to contribute towards the general welfare of society. Islam holds a fundamental principle that woman is a human being, equal to man, and thus has equal rights. Women are equal in their rights to realize their material needs in the world, including similar rights to hold property, mortgage it, bequeath it, sell or buy it, or exploit it for their own benefit. The legal systems of Europe, till very recently, did not give any of these rights to women: she could exercise them only indirectly through a man — her husband, father or guardian. This means that when Islam granted women these rights, the woman in Europe was deprived of them even after more than eleven hundred years. Islam recognizes an independent economic status of woman and gives her the right to own property, use and enjoy it without any intermediary, trustee or mediator. She is free to choose her husband; no marriage is valid unless she agrees to it. Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) says: "No widow should be married without consulting her; and no virgin be married without her assent, and her assent is her silence." Even after the wedding ceremony, if she declares that she does not assent to it, the marriage is dissolved.

The Modern Debate and the West

The furore over the rights of woman and perfect equality with man is raging all across the western countries. A propaganda campaign has been launched against Islamic beliefs and customs by the western media, insisting upon "female emancipation" as essential for the economic and social development of society. The essay says both extremes are wrong: those who claim Islam stands for perfect equality between the two sexes, and those who claim Islam is an enemy of woman that degrades her. A few centuries ago woman was looked upon as a non-entity; scholars debated whether she had a soul or not, and whether she was born as a slave to man. From the inception of civilization down to the period of industrialization, the situation remained unchanged — she was coerced to play the role of a slave. The Industrial Revolution in Europe brought more miseries to woman: she was forced to work in industrial units apart from managing her home; family ties were torn, she was overworked physically, lost respect as well as her womanhood, and could not even win the right to equal wages with man. The European man recognized equal rights for her only after a very tough and intense resistance and a hard struggle.

Feminism and the United Nations

Feminism, a movement for the emancipation of women, is an old movement. The word "Feminism" was first coined by the Younger Dumas in a pamphlet "L'Homme Femme" in 1872. In the early period of the 19th century, women resorted to strikes and non-cooperation, addressed public meetings and employed journalism to advance their cause, which resulted in raising the status of women in the western world. The United Nations declared 1975 as "International Women's Year". Women perform two-thirds of the world's work, receive one-tenth of its income, and own less than one-hundredth of its property. Yet the United Nations is not the first forum which launched a campaign for safeguarding women's rights: about fourteen hundred years ago, Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) presented the first charter of Human Rights, in which women were placed at an equal level with men. He dismantled the concept of women as a necessary evil, a deadly fascination, the devil's gateway. In his Farewell Sermon he said: "O people, it is true that you have certain rights with regard to your women, but they also have rights over you. Do treat your women well and be kind to them, for they are your partners and committed helpers."

The Present Condition

On the other hand, women in the West have in many cases confused liberty with license; liberty without moral and spiritual discipline is a potential dynamite. Even among the advanced countries, after fifty years of struggle, women are still discriminated against in many fields of national life: their representation in political, economic, professional, educational and administrative spheres is not in proportion to their number; in professions like the army, police, architecture and engineering, the entry of women is considered a taboo. In the developing countries their lot is even worse: they are kept away from the mainstream of national life and considered fit only for domestic chores. Islam has been the greatest benefactor of womankind. Robert L. Gulick described Hazrat Muhammad's (peace be upon him) contribution thus: "Muhammad established law and order over a large portion of the known world and anticipated a significant number of the great social movements of the 20th century: equality of opportunity, unrestricted by colour, greater freedom for women, emphasis on universal education, consultation as the bedrock of sound administration, even-handed justice." The preamble to the Declaration on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (November 7, 1967) states that discrimination against woman is incompatible with human dignity and with the welfare of the family and society. Yet in practice, even in Islamic countries, women are still subjected to a slavish existence: tribal customs and traditions contribute towards their degradation; women parliamentarians have never risen above 10% of the total; and statistics obtained at the NGO Forum 1995 indicate that at the current rate of progress it would take 475 years for women to reach equality with men as senior managers in the world.

The Solution

According to the Islamic school of thought, Islam alone provides a solution to the problems of woman no less than that of man. We should turn towards it, strive hard to re-establish an Islamic state and enforce Islamic law in our lives; only then shall we be able to realize in practice our beliefs and ideals — the only way to achieve symmetry and harmony in our life without any resort to injustice and tyranny. Women have to actively work together with men towards gaining equality, but first they must understand the true spirit of the Holy Quran and tailor their demands to it. In the end, the essay quotes Quaid-i-Azam, addressing the audience at Aligarh University in 1944: "No nation can rise to the level of glory unless your women are side by side with you. We are victims of evil customs. It is a crime against humanity that our women are shut up within the four walls of the houses as prisoners. There is no sanction anywhere for the deplorable condition in which our women have to live. You should take your women along with you as comrades in every sphere of life."

Key Points

  • Through history women were denied rights: blamed for sin, kept dependent, buried alive in pre-Islamic Arabia, and treated as property.
  • Islam made woman a full human being with equal rights — to own, sell and bequeath property, and to choose her husband.
  • Europe gave women such rights more than eleven hundred years later, and only after a hard struggle.
  • The Prophet (peace be upon him) presented the first charter of human rights fourteen hundred years ago, placing women equal with men.
  • Even today women are under-represented everywhere; the essay's solution is the true spirit of Islam, and Quaid-i-Azam's call to take women along as comrades in every sphere of life.

lessons.title: Unit 10 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 10 teaches the rules of capitalization, the format of a business letter, and the basics of translation.

Business Letters

A business letter is a letter written from one company or organization to another, or for correspondence between organizations and their customers, clients and other external parties. It is written in formal language, and its overall style depends on the relationship between the organizations. The parts of the format, as labelled in the book's example (a letter to the editor of a magazine about printing an advertisement), are: Heading (sender's name and address — Welfare Educational Society, Shahbaz Town, Quetta), the date (April 21st, 2018), the Inside Address (News Express, 52–F, Jinnah Road, Quetta), the Salutation (Dear Mr. Faheem,), the Body of the letter, the Closing (With warm regards, Thanking you, Yours sincerely,), the Signature, and the writer's name and organization (Nadir Khan, Welfare Educational Society, Quetta). The unit's activity asks for a letter to a company to place an order for stationery material.

Translation

Translation from one language to another is not an easy job. It needs knowledge of both languages; a good command of grammar, vocabulary, idioms and phrases are the basic requirements of translation. Word-for-word translation changes the core concept of the language. The book's examples: "See him off at the station" (an idiom — do not translate word for word); "Work whole-heartedly"; "Talk politely"; "I have known him for a long time"; "He is an apple of his father's eye" (an idiom meaning he is very dear to his father).

Rules of Capitalization — Proper Names

  • Words referring to the Deity: Allah, God, Almighty, Creator, King of kings, Lord (but do not capitalize "god" for pagan deities). Capitalize pronouns that refer to the Deity: God always keeps His promises.
  • Names of Satan, angels, human beings: The Devil, Gabriel, Saima, Fahim, Tariq (the abbreviations Jr. and Sr. are capitalized following a name).
  • Continents, countries, states, provinces, cities: Antarctica, Pakistan, Balochistan, Quetta, Mastung, Lahore.
  • Recognized political or geographical regions: The South, the Far West, the Northwest (U.S.); the Far East, the Near East (but do not capitalize north, east, south, west when they refer to a direction: west of town, driving east). Do not capitalize adjectives that merely indicate a portion of a region: southern France, eastern Balochistan. Do capitalize adjectives that are part of a name of a political or geographical division: Central America, West Germany, Northern Ireland, Eastern Samoa, South Korea, Western Europe.
  • Islands, bodies of water, mountains, parks: Baffin Island, Isle Royale; Old Harbour Bay, Caribbean Sea; Big Horn Mountains, Mount Whitney; Hazar Ganji National Park.
  • Streets and highways: Zaib-un-Nisa Street, Najeeb Street, Forty-second Street (the second part of a hyphenated number is not capitalized).
  • Special organizations: The Security Council, Congress, State Department, Library of Congress, Supreme Court of Pakistan.
  • Calendar items and special events: Friday, May, Eid, Sibi Festival. (Names of the seasons — spring, summer, fall, autumn, winter — are not capitalized unless personified.)
  • Historical events and periods: Hundred Years War, Battle of Panipat, Great Depression, Romantic Age.
  • Nationalities, races and tribes: Pakistani, Dravidian, Bugti, Tareen. Religious writings, groups and terms: The Quran, Hadith, Catholic, Crucifixion. Languages and particular courses: Japanese, Functional English 601, Computer Science 205 (the number after the subject indicates a particular course).
  • Brand names: Dunlop tires, Blue Band (do not capitalize the common noun after the brand name). Monuments, bridges, buildings, documents, planets, ships and other particular things: Death Valley, National Monument, Man Safina, Balochistan Bridge, Habib Plaza.

Titles of Works, and Miscellaneous Rules

Capitalize the first and last words and all content words in the titles of books, magazines, newspapers, poems, stories, plays, musical compositions, paintings, sculpture and other works of art; function words, coordinating conjunctions, prepositions and the articles (a, an, the) are not capitalized: Exploring the World of English (book); News and Views (magazine); Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening (poem); The Merchant of Venice (play). Function words have little meaning on their own but show grammatical relationships (and, to, the) — they are also called grammatical or structural words. Content words refer to a thing, quality, state or action and have meaning when used alone (world, play, happy, quickly) — they are also called lexical words. Miscellaneous rules: (1) capitalize the first word of every sentence, including quoted sentences; (2) capitalize the pronoun "I" and the interjection "O" (the common interjection "oh" is followed by a comma or exclamation point; O is never followed by punctuation); (3) capitalize the first word in every line of poetry, whether or not the word begins a sentence.

The unit's activity paragraph, correctly capitalized: "My lively, funny grandfather, Akbar, lives in Kalat, a quiet suburb of Balochistan, Pakistan. He has occupied the same house for over fifty years. This is my favourite place in the world. Whenever I think of the lush gardens by the house, I feel warm and secure."

Key Points

  • Capitalize proper names: persons, places, organizations, days, months, events, languages, religions and brand names.
  • Do not capitalize seasons or compass directions; do capitalize regions used as names.
  • In titles, capitalize content words only — not articles, prepositions or conjunctions.
  • Always capitalize the pronoun "I", the interjection "O", the first word of a sentence and the first word of each line of poetry.

chapters.title: Unit 11: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam (Poem - Edward FitzGerald)

lessons.title: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam are the famous quatrains (four-line verses, each called a rubai) of the Persian poet Omar Khayyam, translated into English by Edward FitzGerald (1809–1883). FitzGerald was born at Bradfield and educated at Trinity College, Cambridge; he is best known as the poet of the first and most famous English translation of "The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam". The five rubai given in this unit all carry one theme: worldly life, worldly hopes and youth are temporary, and destiny cannot be changed.

Rubai 1: Awake! — the Morning Comes

"AWAKE! For Morning in the Bowl of Night has flung the Stone that puts the Stars to Flight: And Lo! The Hunter of the East has caught the Sultan's Turret in a Noose of Light." In simple words: Wake up! The morning has come into the bowl (cup) of the night like a stone thrown into it, and at its coming the stars have fled away. Look! The sun — the Hunter of the East — has caught the top of the Sultan's palace tower in a rope (noose) made of light. The picture is of sunrise: the first rays of the sun touch the highest tower first, and the stars vanish. It reminds us that a new day — and a new chance — has come, while the night of the past is gone.

Rubai 2: Worldly Hope Is Like Desert Snow

"The Worldly Hope men set their Hearts upon turns Ashes — or it prospers; and anon, like Snow upon the Desert's dusty Face, lighting a little Hour or two — is gone." The hopes of this world on which men fix their hearts either turn to ashes (fail completely) or succeed; but even when they succeed, they last only a very short time — like snow falling on the hot dusty face of a desert, which shines for an hour or two and then melts away and is gone. Worldly hope is compared with desert snow because both vanish very quickly. (The unit's own answers: when the sun rises, the stars vanish/disappear; the snow in the desert vanishes in two hours; worldly hope does not remain forever.)

Rubai 3: The Door Without a Key

"There was a Door to which I found no Key; there was a Veil past which I could not see: some little talk awhile of Me and Thee there seem'd — and then no more of Thee and Me." The poet says there are mysteries of life and the universe — a door — for which he found no key, and a veil (curtain) beyond which he could not see. For a little while there was some talk of "Me and Thee" (man and God, or man and man), and then that talk ended too. The main theme of this rubai is that man cannot solve the mysteries of life and fate; his knowledge is limited and his life is short.

Rubai 4: The Moving Finger

"The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ, moves on: nor all thy Piety nor Wit shall lure it back to cancel half a Line, nor all thy Tears wash out a Word of it." The Moving Finger means fate or destiny — the hand of God that writes our destiny. Once destiny has written something, it moves on and never returns. Neither your piety (religious devotion) nor your wit (intelligence) can bring it back to cancel even half a line, and all your tears cannot wash out a single word of it. The unit's own answer confirms this: we can change our destiny by nothing — not by piety, not by intelligence, not by tears.

Rubai 5: Spring and Youth Pass Away

"Yet Ah, that Spring should vanish with the Rose! That Youth's sweet-scented manuscript should close! The Nightingale that in the branches sang, Ah whence, and whither flown again, who knows!" The poet grieves that spring vanishes along with the rose, and that youth — like a sweet-smelling book (manuscript) — should close so soon. "Manuscript" in this rubai means life (the unit's own answer): the book of youth's life is closed when youth ends. The nightingale that sang in the branches has flown away — from where (whence) it came and to where it has gone, nobody knows. The poet compares spring with youth because both are beautiful and both end very soon; the main theme of this rubai is the shortness of youth and life.

The Lesson of the Rubaiyat

The lesson we get from the Rubaiyat is that this world and everything in it — hopes, youth, beauty and life itself — is temporary. What is written by destiny cannot be changed by piety, wisdom or tears. So we should not spend our lives for worldly gains only; we should value our time and live wisely while the day lasts.

Key Points

  • The Hunter of the East is the sun; its first rays catch the Sultan's turret in a noose of light.
  • Worldly hope is like snow on a desert — it shines for an hour or two and is gone.
  • Man finds no key to the door of life's mysteries and cannot see past the veil.
  • The Moving Finger is destiny: once written, it cannot be cancelled by piety, wit or tears.
  • Youth is a sweet-scented manuscript (the book of life) that closes too soon, like spring with the rose.

lessons.title: Unit 11 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 11 teaches the colon and sentence inversion. It also explains how a writer supports an opinion: the writer or poet presents his or her opinion to persuade the readers, and in order to support the opinion, gives examples and reasons — as Khayyam supports his opinion about the world with the examples of the desert snow, the door without a key and the vanishing spring.

The Colon (:)

  • (a) To introduce a list of items: For the picnic, you should bring these items: three plates, five cups and a knife. (Note: do not use a colon to introduce a list that is the complement of a verb or the object of a preposition — "The items that we should bring for picnic are: three plates…" is incorrect.)
  • (b) To introduce a statement or quotation: William Congreve once made this statement: "Music has charms to soothe the savage beast." (Colon — the quotation is formally announced. When the quotation is not formally introduced, use a comma: It was William Congreve who said, "Music has charms to soothe the savage beast.")
  • (c) Between independent clauses when the second clause explains or summarizes the first: The captain was right: we should have bowled first.
  • (d) Between the chapter and verse of a Quranic reference: Al-Baqara — 2:124; Al-Ibrahim — 14:35.
  • (e) Between the hour and the minute of a time reference: 9:45 a.m., 12:00 a.m., 5:00 p.m.

The unit's activity, with colons placed: (i) Cook these dishes for the party: meat, rice and fish. (ii) The Principal announced the result: Ahmed got first position. (iii) In order to have a safe journey, you should follow these instructions: tie seat belt, drive with normal speed and carefully. (iv) He will arrive at 5:45 p.m. (v) We sell following items: books, notebooks, pencils etc.

Sentence Inversion

Inversion, also known as "anastrophe", is a literary technique in which the normal order of words is reversed in order to achieve a particular effect of emphasis or meter. Inversion is achieved by: placing an adjective after the noun it qualifies (The soldier strong); placing a verb before its subject (Shouts the policeman); placing a noun before its preposition (World between). Some inversions are part of English grammar itself: inversion always occurs in interrogative statements, where verbs or helping verbs are placed before their subjects; and in typical exclamatory sentences, where objects are placed before their verbs and subjects, preceded by a wh-word: What a beautiful picture it is! Where in the world were you! How wonderful the weather is today!

In literature, unusual inversions are employed by writers to achieve special artistic effects. In Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet: "I nursed her daughter that you talked withal" and "he that can lay hold of her shall have the chinks". In Coleridge's Kubla Khan: "In Xanadu did Kubla Khan a stately pleasure-dome decree" — here inversion creates meter and rhyme in the lines ("gardens bright", "forests ancient as the hills"). The main function of inversion in prose or poetry is to help writers achieve a stylistic effect, like laying emphasis on a particular point or changing the focus of the readers; in poetry, inversions are regularly used to create rhythm, meter or a rhyming scheme. In the unit's activity, the inversions are: "What an interesting story this is!"; ""Stop", shouted the king loudly" (verb before subject); "How wonderful the weather is today!"; "To me alone there came a thought of grief" (object first); "How wonderful was he teaching!"

Key Points

  • Use a colon before a list, a formally announced quotation, an explaining clause, in Quranic references (2:124) and in times (9:45).
  • Never put a colon straight after a verb or preposition before a list.
  • Inversion reverses the normal word order for emphasis, meter or rhyme — it is natural in questions and exclamations, and artistic in poetry.

chapters.title: Unit 12: Youth's Participation in Drug Prevention Programmes (Prof. Abdul Majeed Khan)

lessons.title: Youth's Participation in Drug Prevention Programmes — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Youth's Participation in Drug Prevention Programmes, by Prof. Abdul Majeed Khan, explains why young people must take an active part in the fight against drugs. These days drug abuse is becoming an increasing trend; it has become quite common among youth, as drugs have become quite accessible. Today there is a clear need for effective drug prevention programmes directed towards youth.

Youth Are Experts on Their Own Experience

Youth must play an active role in drug prevention programmes. However, it is important to note that youth are not professionals or experts on drugs: they lack experience and knowledge in the academic sense. Of course, they are experts on what they have perceived or even experienced themselves when it comes to discussing the effects of drugs, but they do not know the science behind drugs and drug abuse. Young people have a general knowledge about drugs, but they may not know the specifics — for example, a young person may not know how drugs actually penetrate the human body and which senses they affect first, but an expert in the field of drug abuse could provide the answer. Experts, consultants and professionals can provide support without being in command of a project; more specifically, adults can be a resource for young people when they need any substantiation.

How Adults Should Work with Youth

Occasionally it is difficult for adults to play a supportive role when participating with young people: they often fall into authoritative or imposing roles without even noticing. When working with young people, adults must respect and recognize the value of young people's ideas and opinions. Adults should take them seriously, because young people will equally respect and take seriously what adults say. Adults should also encourage young people to draw upon their skills, knowledge and resources; encouragement can be in the form of a compliment or a reward. Adults should provide their expertise and information when they are needed. Young people must also realize their own benefits from participating with adults: adults have much to share that is relevant to young people's needs — they are able to offer suggestions, resources and, most importantly, vision. However, adults must learn to work with youth rather than telling them what to do. Adults should not press youth into doing or believing something, because youth will realize what the adults are intending and reject it, regardless of its relevance or merit; imposing behaviour often results in irritation and discourages young people from participating.

What Youth Participation Means

Youth participation entails a process through which youth are able to influence and share control over planning, decisions and resources that affect them. At an organizational level, this means being included in decision making, policies and practices in which young people have legitimate roles, such as manager or advisor. On a personal level, participation involves young people's right to be included in, and informed about, decisions and issues affecting their lives. Youth participation means recognizing and fostering youth's influence and ability through their expertise and involvement; only in this way will youth's participation be truly effective for youth themselves, their adult counterparts and the community as a whole.

The Importance of Youth's Participation

Young people have a right to participate in programmes, as enshrined in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 1990; the convention has since been ratified by almost every member state of the UN. One of the principles of the convention states: children must be allowed as active participants in all matters affecting their lives and be free to express their opinions. They have the right to have their views heard and taken seriously.

Drug Prevention Programmes

Drug prevention programmes can target all young people, or they can target specific groups with specific needs, such as young people who have already tried drugs or who are considered "at-risk". Programmes can be held in school or in the community, and they can be run by youth, adults or a combination of both. There is no specific protocol for drug prevention programmes, but in order for them to be effective, programmes should consider the following: enhancing protective factors and reducing risk factors; including skills to resist drugs, strengthening personal commitments against drug use and increasing social competencies; incorporating interactive methods rather than just the traditional educational techniques alone; generating norms that are strengthened against drug use in all kinds of situations; targeting all youth and giving special attention towards identifying those who are most at risk; and being sensitive with respect to ages, cultures and developmental stages.

The Benefits of Youth Participation

Youth participation in drug prevention programmes has great advantages, not only for youth themselves but also for adults and for the community. Since youth are the primary beneficiaries, they gain the most from participation: it is their decisions in managing and implementing policies that improve the programme's objectives, and whatever decisions they make, they will be the ones affected the most. Delivery of services: since young persons are the best experts on young people, they can deliver the best services to them; their involvement makes services more relevant to the needs of young people. Young persons understand each other in a way that is difficult for most adults to comprehend — their behaviour, their style of doing things and even their language differs from adults — so programmes chalked out by young persons are always compatible to the needs of young people. Expressions: participation provides youth an opportunity to share their ideas and experiences on drug abuse; their ideas about the dangers of drugs and methods of prevention often differ from what adults believe, because in some cases young persons have practical experience of drug abuse — they have either been directly affected by drugs, or indirectly affected, as some of their family members have been victims. They can thus provide a better explanation of the effects and hazards of drugs than adults who have never touched any drugs. Skills: by participating, young people gain developmental skills and knowledge that will ensure a better future; they gain experience and confidence after accomplishing a task successfully; leadership roles assigned to them lead them to become responsible citizens; respectable roles groom their personality and let them shoulder responsibilities on their own; and participation gives them the opportunity to channelize their energies for the good of their nation. Communication: the participation of youth allows other youth to feel at ease while speaking on issues in the presence of adults — otherwise they feel shy and hesitate to express their ideas, and some merely ratify the views adults put forward, saying what they think adults want to hear instead of what they really have in their minds, which can be really damaging to a programme. In short, youth participation is all about the development of partnerships between young people and adults across all areas of life, so that young people may take a valued position and play a role in our society, and the community as a whole can benefit from their contribution, ideas and energies.

Key Points

  • Drug abuse is increasing among youth because drugs have become easily accessible.
  • Youth are experts on their own experience of drugs, but not on the science behind them — adults and experts support, not command.
  • Adults must respect young people's ideas and never impose; encouragement may be a compliment or a reward.
  • The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1990) gives children the right to be heard in all matters affecting their lives.
  • Effective programmes enhance protective factors, reduce risk factors, teach resistance skills and use interactive methods.
  • Youth participation benefits everyone: better services, honest expression, leadership skills and easier communication.

lessons.title: Unit 12 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 12 teaches roots, suffixes and prefixes, and the writing process of proofreading and editing.

Root or Base Word

The original word to which a suffix or prefix is added is called a root or base.

Suffixes

A suffix is a letter or a group of letters added at the end of a word. A suffix changes the meaning of the word.

Base wordSuffixNew word
thankfulthankful
carefulcareful

Prefixes

A prefix is a letter or a group of letters added at the beginning of a word. It changes the meaning of the word.

PrefixBase wordNew word
impossibleimpossible
unableunable

The unit's activity asks you to make new words with the prefixes mis- (misunderstand, misbehave), pre- (preview, pre-reading — used in this very book), post- (postpone), tele- (television, telephone) and the suffixes -less (hopeless, careless), -ship (friendship, leadership), -ness (kindness, happiness) and -ment (development, encouragement — both used in this unit).

Proofreading and Editing

The unit's writing activity follows the full writing process: (i) brainstorm your ideas; (ii) make a mind map; (iii) outline your ideas in a logical sequence; (iv) write the essay with the help of the outline; (v) proofread — each student proofreads another's essay, with red ink; (vi) edit it and re-draft it. Before writing, develop focus by identifying your audience and purpose.

Key Points

  • The root is the original word; a prefix is added at the beginning and a suffix at the end — both change the meaning.
  • Examples: im + possible = impossible; care + ful = careful.
  • Good writing is a process: brainstorm, mind map, outline, draft, proofread, edit and re-draft.

lessons.title: Hatchet — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Hatchet is an excerpt from a novel by Gary Paulsen (born 1939), who has written many novels for young readers involving young characters facing challenges. The book's prologue tells us: the main character is a teenager named Brian Robeson. He is on a plane to visit his father in the oil fields in Canada; the only other person on the plane is the pilot. When the pilot has a heart attack, Brian must guide the plane to land. After he lands on a lake, he finds himself alone and scared. The only belongings he has are his clothing and a small axe called a hatchet. Brian must find a way to survive alone in the wilderness. This excerpt shows how Brian makes his first fire.

Sparks but No Fire

Brian found it was a long way from sparks to fire. Clearly there had to be something for the sparks to ignite — some kind of tinder or kindling — but what? He brought some dried grass in, tapped sparks into it and watched them die. He tried small twigs, breaking them into little pieces, but that was worse than the grass. Then he tried a combination of the two, grass and twigs. Nothing. He had no trouble getting sparks, but the tiny bits of hot stone or metal — he couldn't tell which they were — just sputtered and died. He settled back on his haunches in exasperation, looking at the pitiful clump of grass and twigs. He needed something finer — something soft and fine and fluffy to catch the bits of fire. Shredded paper would be nice, but he had no paper. "So close," he said aloud, "so close…"

The Twenty-Dollar Bill and the Birch Trees

He put the hatchet back in his belt and went out of the shelter, limping on his sore leg. There had to be something. Man had made fire; there had been fire for thousands, millions of years; there had to be a way. He dug in his pockets and found the twenty-dollar bill in his wallet. Paper! Worthless paper out here — but if he could get a fire going… He ripped the twenty into tiny pieces, made a pile of pieces, and hit sparks into them. Nothing happened; they just wouldn't take the sparks. But there had to be a way. Not twenty feet to his right, leaning out over the water, were birches. He stood looking at them for a full half-minute before they registered on his mind. They were a beautiful white, with bark like clean, slightly speckled paper. Paper! He moved to the trees. Where the bark was peeling from the trunks, it lifted in tiny tendrils, almost fluffs. Brian plucked some of them loose and rolled them in his fingers: they seemed flammable, dry and nearly powdery. He pulled and twisted bits off the trees, packing them in one hand while he picked and gathered with the other, until he had a wad close to the size of a baseball. Back in the shelter he arranged the ball of birch bark peelings at the base of the black rock and, as an afterthought, threw in the remains of the twenty-dollar bill. He struck, and a stream of sparks fell into the bark and quickly died — but this time one spark fell on one small hair of dry bark, almost a thread of bark, and seemed to glow a bit brighter before it died.

Making a Home for the Sparks

The material had to be finer. There had to be a soft and incredibly fine nest for the sparks. "I must make a home for the sparks," he thought. "A perfect home, or they won't stay; they won't make fire." He started ripping the bark — using his fingernails at first, and when that didn't work, the sharp edge of the hatchet — cutting the bark in thin slivers, hairs so fine they were almost not there. It was painstaking work, slow work, and he stayed with it for over two hours; twice he stopped for a handful of berries and once to go to the lake for a drink. Then back to work, the sun on his back, until at last he had a ball of fluff as big as a grapefruit — dry birch bark fluff. He positioned his spark nest — as he thought of it — at the base of the rock, used his thumb to make a small depression in the middle, and slammed the back of the hatchet down across the black rock. A cloud of sparks rained down, most of them missing the nest, but some — perhaps thirty or so — hit in the depression, and of those, six or seven found fuel and grew, smouldered, and caused the bark to take on a red glow. Then they went out. Close — he was close. He repositioned the nest, made a new and smaller dent with his thumb, and struck again. More sparks, a slight glow, then nothing. "It's me," he thought. "I'm doing something wrong. I do not know this — a cave dweller would have had a fire by now, a Cro-Magnon man would have a fire by now — but I don't know this. I don't know how to make a fire." Maybe not enough sparks. He settled the nest in place once more and hit the rock with a series of blows, as fast as he could. The sparks poured like a golden waterfall. At first they seemed to take — there were several, many sparks that found life and took briefly — but they all died. Starved.

The Missing Thing: Air

He leaned back. "They are like me. They are starving." It wasn't quantity — there were plenty of sparks — but they needed more. "I would kill," he thought suddenly, "for a book of matches. Just one book. Just one match. I would kill." What makes fire? He thought back to school, to all those science classes. You have to have fuel — and he had that; the bark was fuel. Oxygen — there had to be air. He needed to add air; he had to fan on it, blow on it. He made the nest ready again, held the hatchet backward, tensed, and struck four quick blows. Sparks came down and he leaned forward as fast as he could and blew. Too hard! There was a bright, almost intense glow — then it was gone. He had blown it out. Another set of strikes, more sparks. He leaned and blew, but gently this time, holding back and aiming the stream of air from his mouth to hit the brightest spot. Five or six sparks had fallen in a tight mass of bark hair, and Brian centered his efforts there. The sparks grew with his gentle breath. The red glow moved from the sparks themselves into the bark, moved and grew and became worms — glowing red worms that crawled up the bark hairs and caught other threads of bark and grew, until there was a pocket of red as big as a quarter, a glowing red coal of heat. And when he ran out of breath and paused to inhale, the red ball suddenly burst into flame. "Fire!" he yelled. "I've got fire! I've got it, I've got it, I've got it…"

Key Points

  • Brian, alone in the Canadian wilderness with only a hatchet, must make fire to survive.
  • Sparks alone are not enough: grass, twigs and even his twenty-dollar bill will not catch them.
  • Birch bark, ripped into hair-fine fluff over two painstaking hours, makes a "nest" — a home for the sparks.
  • The sparks still starve until Brian remembers his science lessons: fire needs fuel and oxygen.
  • Blowing gently — not too hard — grows the red coal until it bursts into flame: patience and thinking, not strength, win.

lessons.title: Unit 13 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The book's Glossary explains the difficult words of this story. The unit also teaches you to deduce the meaning of difficult words from context: the context of a word is the other words around it — for example, in "the sparks just sputtered and died", the word "died" helps you guess what "sputtered" means. Learn these words with their meanings and their use in the story.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
sparksSmall fiery particles thrown off from a fire. Brian strikes sparks from the black rock with his hatchet.
sputteredMade a series of soft explosive sounds. The tiny bits of hot stone or metal just sputtered and died.
on his haunchesSitting on his heels, in a squatting position. He settled back on his haunches in exasperation.
exasperationThe feeling of being annoyed or irritated. Brian felt exasperation when the sparks kept dying.
pitifulDeserving pity; very small and poor. The pitiful clump of grass and twigs would not catch fire.
tendrilsThin, curly threads. The peeling birch bark lifted in tiny tendrils, almost fluffs.
wadA lump or bundle of a soft material. He gathered a wad of bark close to the size of a baseball.
painstakingDone with great care and thoroughness. Ripping the bark into fine hairs was painstaking work of over two hours.
Cro-Magnon manAn early human. Brian thinks even a Cro-Magnon man would have made a fire by now.
tensedBecame tense; stiffened the muscles. He held the hatchet backward, tensed, and struck four quick blows.
positionedPut in a particular place. He positioned his spark nest at the base of the rock.

The unit's own answers: Brian is lost in the woods with only a hatchet as a tool; Brian wanted to have a fire; Brian moved to the trees to pluck fluffy bark; Brian wanted to find out the way how to burn fire (make a fire); and when Brian ran out of breath and paused to inhale, the red ball burst into flames. A depression is a sunken place or hollow — Brian used his thumb to make a small depression in the middle of the spark nest.

Key Points

  • Use the words around a new word — its context — to guess its meaning.
  • Tinder must be soft, fine and fluffy to catch sparks.
  • Fire needs three things together: sparks, fuel and air (oxygen).

lessons.title: Unit 13 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 13 has no grammar section; its language work is using context to understand vocabulary, and its writing work is the job application, resume (curriculum vitae) and covering letter, with tips for a job interview.

Using Context to Understand Vocabulary

The context of a word is the other words around it. You can use the context to help you understand new words. The book's example: in "Hatchet", the sparks made by Brian "just sputtered and died" — you can use the word "died" to guess what "sputtered" means; the word "died" is context for "sputtered". The unit's activity asks you to guess the meanings of exasperation, pitiful, registered, tendrils, wad, painstaking, positioned and tensed from their context in the story — all of these are explained in this unit's Word Meanings lesson.

Curriculum Vitae (CV) and Resume

A curriculum vitae is a summary of an applicant's professional experience and educational background, along with other relevant information regarding the candidate's qualifications. The curriculum vitae is similar to a résumé, but is used more frequently by candidates who have published works in journals, such as scientists or academic professionals. The book's CV format is: Name (with Address and Cell No.); Personal Information (Father's Name, Date of Birth, Nationality, Domicile, CNIC No., Religion, Marital Status); Objective; Academic Qualification (a table: Education | Year | Institution | Marks); Work Experience; Languages; Extracurricular Activities and Interests; Reference. When you apply for a job advertised in a newspaper or elsewhere, you send a job application or covering letter with your CV: the covering letter introduces you, names the post you are applying for, and briefly says why you are suitable.

Tips for Giving a Job Interview

An interview is a series of questions and answers: the interviewer asks the questions, and the interviewee answers them; the interview usually gives information about the interviewee's life, experience or opinions. The book's tips are: (1) Conduct research on the employer, hiring manager and job opportunity — understand the employer, the requirements of the job and the background of the person interviewing you. (2) Review common interview questions and prepare your responses; practise orally. (3) Dress for success: wear neat and clean clothes and polished shoes; do not smoke or eat right before the interview; brush your teeth or use mouthwash. (4) Arrive on time, relaxed and prepared — strive to arrive about 15 minutes before your scheduled interview; arriving early is also a chance to observe the dynamics of the workplace. (5) Make good first impressions: be polite and offer warm greetings to everyone you meet. (6) Be authentic, upbeat, focused, confident and concise: respond truthfully, provide solid examples of solutions and accomplishments, but keep responses short and to the point. (7) Remember the importance of body language: smiling, eye contact, solid posture, active listening and nodding. (8) Thank the interviewer(s): common courtesy and politeness go far in interviewing; thank each person who interviewed you before you leave.

Key Points

  • Guess new words from context — the words around them.
  • A CV summarizes your personal information, objective, qualifications, experience, languages, interests and references.
  • For an interview: research, prepare answers, dress neatly, arrive 15 minutes early, mind your body language, and thank the interviewers.

lessons.title: If — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
If is the famous poem by Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936), the English journalist, short-story writer, poet and novelist, author of "The Jungle Book" (1894) and "Kim" (1901). The poem "If" was written in 1910. In the poem the speaker is a father, and the poem is addressed to his son ("you'll be a Man, my son!"). The father gives his son advice about how to face life: every line begins with a condition — "If you can…" — which is why the poem is titled "If". If the son follows all this advice, he will win the Earth and, what is more, he will be a true Man.

Stanza 1: Keep Calm, Trust Yourself, Be Patient and Honest

"If you can keep your head when all about you are losing theirs and blaming it on you" — stay calm and sensible when everyone around you is panicking and blaming you for the trouble; people should keep calm in difficult situations because panic makes things worse, while a cool head finds the way out. "If you can trust yourself when all men doubt you, but make allowance for their doubting too" — have faith in yourself even when others doubt you, yet understand their doubts and do not be angry with them. "If you can wait and not be tired by waiting" — be patient and work hard while waiting for the result. "Or being lied about, don't deal in lies" — if people tell lies about you, do not answer with lies; never lie, even if people lie about us. "Or being hated, don't give way to hating" — people may hate us, but we should not hate them. "And yet don't look too good, nor talk too wise" — and with all these virtues, do not show off or pretend to be very good or very wise.

Stanza 2: Dreams, Triumph and Disaster, Rebuilding

"If you can dream — and not make dreams your master" — dream big, but do not let dreams rule you; the poet suggests his son should dream but not make the dreams his master. "If you can think — and not make thoughts your aim" — think deeply, but do not stop at thinking; act also. "If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster and treat those two impostors just the same" — success (Triumph) and failure (Disaster) are both impostors, deceivers: success does not last and failure does not last either, so treat them equally; do not be too proud in success or too sad in failure — the poet wants them treated the same because life is a combination of success and failure, and neither is the true, permanent reality. "If you can bear to hear the truth you've spoken twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools" — bear it patiently when wicked men twist your true words to trap foolish people. "Or watch the things you gave your life to, broken, and stoop and build 'em up with worn-out tools" — if the work of your whole life is destroyed, bend down and build it again, even with old, worn-out tools; never give up.

Stanza 3: Risk Everything, Hold On, Stay Humble

"If you can make one heap of all your winnings and risk it on one turn of pitch-and-toss, and lose, and start again at your beginnings and never breathe a word about your loss" — if you lose everything in one gamble, start again from the very beginning without complaining or telling anyone about your loss. "If you can force your heart and nerve and sinew to serve your turn long after they are gone, and so hold on when there is nothing in you except the Will which says to them: 'Hold on!'" — when your body is exhausted, let your willpower drive you to hold on. "If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue, or walk with Kings — nor lose the common touch" — mix with common people without losing your goodness, and move with kings without forgetting ordinary people. "If neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you; if all men count with you, but none too much" — value everyone, but depend on no one too much.

Stanza 4: Use Every Minute

"If you can fill the unforgiving minute with sixty seconds' worth of distance run" — time does not forgive the person who wastes it; use every minute fully, as a runner uses every second of a race. Then comes the reward: "Yours is the Earth and everything that's in it, and — which is more — you'll be a Man, my son!" The poet uses comparisons and contrasts throughout the poem — Triumph against Disaster, crowds against Kings, foes against loving friends, dreaming against thinking — to explain his thoughts: in every opposite situation of life, the son must keep the same balance.

Key Points

  • The speaker is a father advising his son; the title "If" comes from the conditions ("If you can…") on which manhood depends.
  • Keep calm under blame, trust yourself, wait patiently, never lie and never hate.
  • Dream and think, but let neither rule you; treat Triumph and Disaster — both impostors — just the same.
  • If your life's work breaks, build it up again; if you lose everything, start again silently.
  • Fill every unforgiving minute with work — then the Earth is yours, and you will be a Man.

lessons.notes_html:
The book's Glossary explains the difficult words of this poem. Learn these words with their meanings and their use in the poem.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
ImpostorA person who pretends to be someone else in order to deceive others. Triumph and Disaster are called two impostors because neither of them is permanent or real.
knaveA dishonest or unscrupulous man. Knaves twist the truth you have spoken to make a trap for fools.
sinewA piece of tough fibrous tissue uniting muscle to bone; a tendon or ligament. "Force your heart and nerve and sinew to serve your turn" — use every part of your body's strength.

More expressions from the poem: pitch-and-toss is a game of chance — risking everything on one turn of it means gambling all you have on one chance; worn-out tools are old, used-up instruments — building again with them means starting again with whatever little you have left; and the unforgiving minute is time, which never excuses the one who wastes it.

Key Points

  • An impostor pretends to be what he is not — success and failure both deceive us.
  • A knave is a dishonest man; sinews are the tough tissues joining muscle to bone.
  • The poem's advice is conditional: follow it, and "you'll be a Man, my son!"

lessons.title: Unit 14 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 14 teaches the comma, and explains the narrative incident and summarizing a text.

Narrative Incident and Summary

A narrative tells about things that happen. The features of a personal narrative are: Experiences — the author's life, thoughts and feelings; Details — words that describe true information, things and actions; Pronouns — use of I, we, us or me; Structure — paragraphs. Summarizing is the gist of the original text: it provides the main points of the text and avoids unnecessary description and details.

The Comma — the Rule of Thumb

The comma is perhaps the most puzzling mark of punctuation. A useful rule of thumb is: a comma indicates a pause in speech. When in doubt, read the sentence aloud; if you pause at some place, insert a comma to mark the pause. Compare: "Historically the comma is derived from the diagonal slash which was used to indicate a pause" (incorrect) with "Historically, the comma is derived from the diagonal slash, which was used to indicate a pause" (correct).

The Six Rules for the Comma

  • Rule 1 — in a series of three or more items (normally the last item is preceded by and, or, or nor): The new regulations concern students, research fellows, and post-doctoral researchers.
  • Rule 2 — to separate two or more coordinate adjectives (coordinate adjectives describe the noun separately): It was a dark, stormy night. The new headmaster is a tall, good-looking man.
  • Rule 3 — to separate independent clauses introduced by and, or, nor, but, yet, for, so: The rain poured down, and Asif looked for a shelter. Maria handed in the application, but she was not satisfied. (Be careful: use a comma only when the part after and/or/but is a full clause; if it is not, no comma: The rain poured down and ruined the parade.)
  • Rule 4 — after an introductory phrase or word: In the event of disagreement about the duties, the work plan may be presented to the Ph.D Committee. Nevertheless, the students performed poorly. On Tuesday, the Prime Minister met the demonstrators.
  • Rule 5 — after a dependent clause preceding an independent clause: If Sami accepts our conditions, we will agree to the proposal.
  • Rule 6 — before and after parts of the sentence that are not essential to its meaning: such non-essential parts can be words, phrases and entire clauses; test by leaving the part out and seeing whether the message changes grammatically: Our experimental data, however, show that the previous results are unreliable, at best. The audience, indifferent at the beginning, became more and more interested. In 1888, when my great grandmother was born, there was only one hospital in the entire country. Do not use commas to separate essential parts of the sentence.

The unit's activity, with commas placed: (i) After it rained, he didn't go out. (ii) Undoubtedly, we have won the match. (iii) It was a funny, interesting movie. (iv) He brought a pen, a marker and an eraser. (v) Ali, who is teaching English, is my brother.

Key Points

  • A comma marks a pause in speech — read aloud when in doubt.
  • Use commas in lists, between coordinate adjectives, before conjunctions joining full clauses, after introductions, and around non-essential parts.
  • A summary keeps only the main points; a personal narrative uses I/we and true details from the author's life.

lessons.title: And Now Miguel — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
And Now Miguel is a play by Joseph Krumgold (1908–1980), the American writer of novels, children's books and screenplays. His books tell stories about growing up and how we learn to accept and respect one another; in 1966 his book about Miguel Chavez was made into the movie "And Now Miguel". The play has eight scenes, and Miguel himself is the narrator of his own story.

Scene 1: Miguel Wants to Be a Man

Miguel introduces himself: "I am Miguel Chavez. To my family, I am just a boy. But I want to be a man. The men in my family raise sheep in the mountains of New Mexico. It has been our work for hundreds of years. I, too, will be a shepherd someday. I hope and I wait. But 'someday' never comes." Miguel and his elder brother Gabriel are driving out to the new pasture, and Miguel is quiet. Gabriel asks, "What's up, Miguel?" Miguel says he has been thinking how easy it is for Gabriel to be Gabriel — but it is not easy for him to be Miguel. Gabriel laughs: it takes a little time; wait a year or two and it will be easier. Miguel asks if there isn't something he can do now, like practice. Gabriel shakes his head: "Being Miguel — it's not like playing basketball. As I say, it takes time."

Scene 2: Painting Numbers on the Sheep

Miguel tells us his wish: to take the sheep into the Sangre de Cristo Mountains along with the other men. If the men know you are ready, you will go; but if they don't, you must wait again for another year. "I must try to make them see that I am ready." The first lamb of the year is born, and before long there are many new lambs. Miguel gets the job of painting numbers on the sheep — that way it is easy to tell which lamb belongs to which mother in case they get separated. During a break, his grandfather speaks to him: "That's the real work of a pastor, of a shepherd — to see that no sheep strays away from the flock. All must stay together." Miguel asks why sheep go off by themselves — why are sheep so dumb? Grandfather laughs: "Sheep are like people." When people don't stick together, they get lost.

Scene 3: The Lost Sheep

Some boys dream of becoming policemen or airplane pilots, but for Miguel there is only one kind of work: at night he looks at the mountains and dreams of becoming a shepherd. One night there is a storm; the next morning, more than a dozen sheep are gone. At breakfast Miguel offers excitedly: "I can find them! I can help!" But Father sends him to school: "This is not a job for you." At school, a boy named Juby tells Miguel he saw the sheep — in the opposite direction from where the others planned to look. Miguel thinks quickly: if he came home with the missing sheep, the men would have to say he is ready. He doesn't look back as he runs down the hill, away from the school. Miguel searches for hours; he is tired and his feet hurt, and he is about to give up — when he spots the sheep coming up the hill towards him.

Scene 4: School Is More Important than Sheep

A little while later, Miguel arrives home with the sheep. "Bravo!" the men shout. But Father has something to say: "I am glad that the sheep are back. Sheep are important. But school is even more important. If you stayed away from school every time something had to be done, you'd grow up to be a burro (a donkey — an uneducated person)." Miguel understands. Father smiles and thanks him for what he did. Later, Miguel tries to ask his father about going up to the mountains when school is over. Father says firmly: "No! It cannot be arranged. Not this year. Gabriel will go. That is part of his work. It's not yet time for you to go." That night, Miguel prays to San Ysidro: "If you think it is a good idea, please arrange it so I may go up into the Sangre de Cristo Mountains."

Scene 5: The Sack of Fleeces

It's June. After the sheep are sheared, the flock will leave for the mountains. During the shearing, Miguel sweeps the floor. He explains proudly: it is a big job to be the one with the broom — when the fleeces come off the sheep they fall on the floor, and if they get dirty the buyer is disappointed, so the floor has to be swept in the best and most careful way. "My father trusts me to do a good job. Maybe he believes I'm becoming a man." Miguel is a hard worker, and the men praise him because he sweeps up so much dust. But suddenly one day Miguel slips and falls into the bottom of a big sack of fleeces. Eli calls out, "Did anyone see Miguel?" Gabriel, looking down in the sack, answers: "Here! He's in the sack!" All the men yell and laugh — except Miguel's father, who snaps: "Is this any time to start playing games, like you were a little boy? Now come on! Up!" Miguel says: "I was ashamed. I no longer felt like a man. If I could have stayed at the bottom of the sack, I would have stayed there."

Scenes 6–8: The Wish Comes True — in a Surprising Way

Two days later, Father has news: "You will go with us to the mountains, Miguel — for the whole summer." Miguel is puzzled and glad. "How did this happen?" Father explains: "Gabriel can't go. He has to go into the army to train to be a soldier. There was a letter this morning." Miguel stands there quietly; he does not know what to think — there was too much good mixed up with the bad. Miguel feels terrible: he thinks it is because of his prayers that Gabriel has to go away. Finally the brothers talk together. Gabriel says: "It's dangerous to wish so hard, Miguel. Sometimes wishes come true in ways that surprise you." Miguel says he is sorry. But Gabriel answers: "I made a wish, too. For a long time, I have wished to see other places, like an ocean. Now I have my wish." Miguel understands. Gabriel tells him: "While I'm gone, Miguel, you learn everything about sheep. When I come back, you and I will be the best two pastors in all New Mexico." Miguel smiles: "I promise." The next morning Miguel left with the men for the mountains, and Gabriel left for the army. Five days later they reached their camp, high up in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains. Many men named Chavez had come to this place. "And now, watching the country below, I, Miguel, stood there at last."

Key Points

  • Miguel Chavez, a shepherd's son in New Mexico, longs to be treated as a man and to go with the men to the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.
  • He paints numbers on the sheep, finds the lost sheep by himself, and sweeps the shearing floor with great care.
  • Father teaches him two lessons: sheep must stay together like people, and school is even more important than sheep.
  • His wish comes true only because Gabriel is called to the army — wishes can come true in surprising, mixed ways.
  • Gabriel also gets his own wish — to see other places, like an ocean — and Miguel finally stands in the mountains: "And now Miguel."

lessons.notes_html:
Unit 15 teaches direct and indirect speech. Its writing work is a research report (brainstorm, outline, collect information, write, proofread and re-draft — the same steps as Unit 1).

Direct and Indirect Speech

When we report the actual words of a speaker, we use direct speech: He said, "I am tired." Naeem said, "Asma studies daily." When we say or report what the speaker said without quoting his exact words, we use indirect speech: He said that he was tired. Naeem said that Asma studied daily.

Changes of Tenses in Indirect Speech

  • Present Simple → Past Simple: He said, "I write a book." → He said that he wrote a book.
  • Present Continuous → Past Continuous: He said, "He is watching a movie." → He said that he was watching a movie.
  • Present Perfect → Past Perfect: She said, "He has done his job." → She said that he had done his job.
  • Present Perfect Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous: He said, "I have been playing since 3 o'clock." → He said that he had been playing since 3 o'clock.
  • Past Simple → Past Perfect: He said to me, "You behaved well." → He said to me that I had behaved well.
  • Past Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous: They said, "We were enjoying the drama." → They said that they had been enjoying the drama.
  • Past Perfect → Past Perfect (no change): She said, "She had consulted a doctor." → She said that she had consulted a doctor.
  • Future Simple: will → would: He said, "I will study very hard." → He said that he would study very hard.
  • Future Continuous: will be → would be: I said to him, "I will be writing to him." → I said to him that I would be writing to him.
  • Future Perfect: will have → would have: He said, "I will have completed the work." → He said that he would have completed the work.

The Unit's Activity — Worked Answers

  • She said, "He goes to office daily." → She said that he went to office daily.
  • She said, "I am washing my dishes." → She said that she was washing her dishes.
  • He said, "I have written a book." → He said that he had written a book.
  • She said, "It has been raining for three days." → She said that it had been raining for three days.
  • Ibrahim said, "They went to cinema." → Ibrahim said that they had gone to cinema.
  • He said to me, "I was waiting for you." → He said to me that he had been waiting for me.
  • He said, "I had started a campaign." → He said that he had started a campaign.
  • He said, "I will buy a mobile." → He said that he would buy a mobile.
  • She said, "I will be singing a song." → She said that she would be singing a song.
  • She said, "They will have achieved the target." → She said that they would have achieved the target.

Key Points

  • Direct speech quotes the exact words inside inverted commas; indirect speech reports them with "that" and changes the tense one step back.
  • Will becomes would; the past perfect never changes.
  • Pronouns change with the reporter: "I" in direct speech becomes he/she in indirect speech.

lessons.title: It Couldn't Be Done — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
It Couldn't Be Done is an inspiring poem by Edgar Albert Guest (1881–1959), the English-born American poet known as the "People's Poet". His poems had an inspirational and optimistic view of everyday life; "It Couldn't Be Done", "Life" and "Don't Quit" are three of his most inspiring and motivating poems. The poem's theme is simple: never say a thing cannot be done until you have tried it.

Stanza 1: He Wouldn't Say So Till He'd Tried

"Somebody said that it couldn't be done, but he, with a chuckle, replied that 'maybe it couldn't', but he would be one who wouldn't say so till he'd tried." Somebody declared a task impossible. The man in the poem only laughed (chuckled) and answered politely: perhaps it cannot be done — but he will not say that until he has tried it himself. This is how the character is optimistic: he does not accept failure before trying. "So he buckled right in with the trace of a grin on his face. If he worried, he hid it. He started to sing as he tackled the thing that couldn't be done — and he did it!" He set to work cheerfully, with a smile; if he had any worry, he hid it; singing as he worked, he tackled the impossible task — and accomplished it.

Stanza 2: He Began It at Once

"Somebody scoffed: 'Oh, you'll never do that; at least no one ever has done it.'" Somebody mocked him: nobody has ever done this, so you will never do it either. "But he took off his coat and he took off his hat, and the first thing we knew, he'd begun it." Without wasting time in argument, he removed his coat and hat — he got ready for hard work — and immediately began. "With a lift of his chin and a bit of a grin, without any doubting or quiddit, he started to sing as he tackled the thing that couldn't be done — and he did it!" A "quiddit" is a useless excuse or quibble; he had no doubts and no excuses. After accomplishing the difficult task, his attitude was the same cheerful confidence — he sang as he worked, and succeeded.

Stanza 3: The Poet Speaks to Us

"There are thousands to tell you it cannot be done; there are thousands to prophesy failure; there are thousands to point out to you, one by one, the dangers that wait to assail you." In life, thousands of people will discourage us about doing a difficult task: they predict failure and list all the dangers waiting to attack us. People discourage us because they judge a task by their own fears, or because no one has done it before. "But just buckle in with a bit of a grin, just take off your coat and go to it; just start in to sing as you tackle the thing that 'cannot be done' — and you'll do it." The poet's advice: smile, prepare yourself, begin cheerfully — and you will do the thing that "cannot be done".

Key Points

  • The character never says a task is impossible before trying it — that is his optimism.
  • He hides his worry, sings as he works, and makes no excuses (no "quiddit").
  • Thousands of people will prophesy failure and point out dangers; do not listen to them.
  • The recipe for success: buckle in with a grin, take off your coat, begin at once — and you'll do it.

Words and Meanings

perseverancePersistence in doing something despite difficulty or delay in achieving success. The man in the poem succeeds by perseverance — he keeps trying cheerfully until the thing is done.

More words from the poem: to scoff is to mock or laugh with contempt ("Somebody scoffed: 'Oh, you'll never do that'"); to prophesy is to predict what will happen; to assail is to attack; to buckle in (or buckle down) is to set to work with determination; a chuckle is a quiet laugh; and a quiddit is a trivial excuse or quibble — the man worked "without any doubting or quiddit". lessons.title: Unit 16 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 16 teaches the semicolon (;). Its writing work is a persuasive essay (for example, "Education is the key to success"), using the persuasive-essay qualities given in Unit 3.

The Four Uses of the Semicolon

  • 1. Between independent clauses when you do not use a comma and a coordinating conjunction. (The coordinating conjunctions are and, but, or, either…or, neither…nor, for, yet.) Example (Plato): "Punishment brings wisdom; it is the healing art of wickedness."
  • 2. Between independent clauses even with a coordinating conjunction, (1) if there are commas within the clauses, or (2) if the clauses are long. This semicolon is often necessary to make clear the major break between independent clauses. Example (Plato): "Ignorance of all things is an evil neither terrible nor excessive, nor yet the greatest of all; but great cleverness and much learning, if they be accompanied by a bad training, are a much greater misfortune."
  • 3. Between independent clauses joined by transitional words, such as accordingly, consequently, for example, for instance, however, namely, nevertheless, that is, then, therefore, thus. (These words are not equivalent to coordinating conjunctions.) Example: Islam teaches that cleanliness is half of faith; thus, we should keep ourselves clean.
  • 4. Between items in a series if the items themselves contain commas. Example: The names of three universities in Balochistan: University of Balochistan, Quetta; University of Turbat, Makran; and University of Loralai, Zhob.

Key Points

  • A semicolon joins two complete, closely related clauses — it is stronger than a comma and weaker than a full stop.
  • Use it before transitional words like however, therefore and thus when they join two clauses.
  • Use semicolons to separate list items that already contain commas.
